# The Army of the Upright

https://queering.earth/on-being-ill
The readings · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/)

Sheet · a reading

# The Army of the Upright

**Specimen**
: *On Being Ill*

**Maker**
: Virginia Woolf

**First printed**
: *The New Criterion*, January 1926

**This text**
: The Hogarth Press, 1930 — revised by Woolf, and set in type by her

**Read**
: 7 September 2026

**Read by**
: [Helen Edgar](https://morerealms.com/) and Ryan Boren

Woolf wrote the essay about illness that English did not have, complained inside it that English could not hold one, and then went back four years later and quietly made her own sentences stranger. This sheet mounts the text as she left it in 1930.

## Illness has no place in literature

The essay opens with a list of what a temperature does to a person — the undiscovered countries, the wastes and deserts of the soul, the ancient and obdurate oaks uprooted by a bout of flu — and then lands on a complaint about the shelf:

Specimen — the missing theme

> …it becomes strange indeed that illness has not taken its place with love and battle and jealousy among the prime themes of literature.

Virginia Woolf, *On Being Ill*, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

Novels devoted to influenza, she says; epic poems to typhoid; odes to pneumonia, lyrics to tooth-ache. It is a joke and it is not a joke. Love and battle and jealousy are the themes that got the canon, and every one of them is something a body does while upright and in motion. The condition that stops the body is the one the shelf has no room for.

This is a claim about literature, and it is also a claim about who gets to be a subject. A century of Disabled and chronically ill writers have made the second claim directly. Woolf makes the first, in 1926, and leaves the second sitting underneath it.

## The language runs dry

Her explanation for the gap is not squeamishness. It is vocabulary.

Specimen — the poverty of the language

> English, which can express the thoughts of Hamlet and the tragedy of Lear, has no words for the shiver and the headache. It has all grown one way.

Virginia Woolf, *On Being Ill*, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

**It has all grown one way.** A language is a record of what its speakers were required to be able to say. Hamlet got four centuries of vocabulary; the shiver got none. So the person in the bed is left, in Woolf's account, with nothing ready made — forced to “coin words himself, and, taking his pain in one hand, and a lump of pure sound in the other… so to crush them together that a brand new word in the end drops out.”

She then does it herself. Chloral hydrate, the sedative she reaches for, arrives in the essay as “that mighty Prince with the moths' eyes and the feathered feet, one of whose names is Chloral” — a mythological figure invented on the spot because the pharmacological name will not carry what the drug means at four in the morning.

**Where we take this next is ours and not hers.** Coining words for what the language has no room for is exactly what Autistic and Disabled communities have spent decades doing — [monotropism](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/monotropism/), [neuroqueer](https://neuroqueer.com/), bodymind, spoons. Woolf is describing one sufferer, one headache, and one doctor in the nineteen-twenties. She is not anticipating a lexicon that people would build a hundred years later out of their own lives. Reading her sentence forward to meet it is our move. The observation that the language grew one way is hers.

## Deserters

Then comes the sentence this sheet is named for. Woolf has been describing the effort health demands — the genial pretence, the endless obligation to communicate and share and work together — and the moment it stops:

Specimen — the army of the upright

> Directly the bed is called for, or, sunk deep among pillows in one chair, we raise our feet even an inch above the ground on another, we cease to be soldiers in the army of the upright; we become deserters. They march to battle.

Virginia Woolf, *On Being Ill*, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

Normativity, named as a posture. Not a belief, not an attitude — a way of holding the body that the rest of it is conscripted into. *The army of the upright.* Vertical, mobile, productive, on time. An inch of foot above the floor is enough to break the enlistment.

What makes the sentence hold is that Woolf does not treat desertion as defeat. The deserter is the one who can finally “look round, to look up—to look, for example, at the sky.” The upright never see it: their sky is “mutilated by chimneys and churches” and serves as a background for man. Lying down is what gives it back.

An essay that had only complained about being ill would not be on this site. This one says the position everyone is arranged into is a position, and that leaving it lets you see.

## The body intervenes

Underneath both arguments is a third, and it is the one that has aged least:

Specimen — a sheet of plain glass

> …literature does its best to maintain that its concern is with the mind; that the body is a sheet of plain glass through which the soul looks straight and clear, and, save for one or two passions such as desire and greed, is null, and negligible and non-existent. On the contrary, the very opposite is true. All day, all night the body intervenes.

Virginia Woolf, *On Being Ill*, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

The creature within, she writes, can only gaze through the pane — smudged or rosy — and cannot separate off from the body “like the sheath of a knife or the pod of a pea for a single instant.” That is a refusal of the mind–body split, written plainly, decades before the word *bodymind* was available to say it in one breath. Again: the word is not hers, and we are not putting it in her mouth. The refusal is.

## What this sheet will not tidy

The same essay is snobbish about the people doing the caring, and it reaches for empire when it wants a figure for effort.

Sympathy, Woolf writes, is “dispensed chiefly by the laggards and failures, women for the most part… who, having dropped out of the race, have time to spend upon fantastic and unprofitable excursions.” She then names three of them by their initials, with real affection — the friend who builds up the nursery fender by the sickroom fire, the one who would ransack London for a giant tortoise to solace you. They are the reason the essay exists. They are also, in her sentence, the ones who lost.

And the labour of staying upright is “to communicate, to civilise, to share, to cultivate the desert, educate the native, to work together by day and by night to sport.” The desert and the native are doing figurative work in a list about going to the office. That is the imperial imagination supplying a metaphor without being asked, in 1926, in a sentence about being tired.

Neither of these is a reason to put the essay down, and neither gets softened here. An essay can see the arrangement of the upright with total clarity from inside the bed and still not see the arrangement of the sickroom it is lying in — who is paid, who is unpaid, who is a woman, who dropped out of a race she was never going to be allowed to win. **Woolf is describing care work as the occupation of people with nothing better to do, while being kept alive by it.** The sharpest reading of normativity in the essay is the one it does not turn on itself.

## She revised her own sentence

One more thing, and it is the reason this sheet names its edition on the label.

*On Being Ill* exists in two states Woolf authorised. It appeared in *The New Criterion* in January 1926, and she revised it for the Hogarth Press edition of 1930 — two hundred and fifty signed copies, the type set by her. The revisions are not corrections. In the first paragraph alone:

The first paragraph, 1926 and 1930

| 1926, *The New Criterion* | 1930, The Hogarth Press |
| --- | --- |
| brings to *light* | brings to *view* |
| uprooted in us *in* the act of sickness | uprooted in us *by* the act of sickness |
| when we think of this *and infinitely more* | when we think of this |
| with love*,* battle*,* and jealousy | with love *and* battle *and* jealousy |
| is null*,* negligible and non-existent | is null*, and* negligible and non-existent |

Look at the last two. In 1926 those are lists, punctuated the way a list is supposed to be punctuated. In 1930 the commas open out into *and…and…and*, and the sentences stop being tidy. Love and battle and jealousy arrive one after another with no rest between them. Null, and negligible and non-existent piles up instead of resolving.

It is the same move the essay is about. A writer who has just argued that the language grew one way went back into her own prose and un-grew it a little — in the direction of the breath, and away from the rule. She did it four years later, in type she set with her own hands, on a page she owned outright because the press was hers.

**So the edition is not a footnote here.** Quote the 1926 commas and you are quoting Woolf. Quote the 1930 *and…and…and* and you are also quoting Woolf. Quote one and date it to the other and you have made a claim about her that is not true. This sheet reads 1930 because the revision is part of what it is reading. The 1926 text is [scanned and online](https://thenewcriterion1926.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/12/woolf-on-being-ill.pdf), and it is worth putting beside this one.

## In their indifference

The essay ends up among flowers, because the deserter, flat on her back, has time to look at them properly. Woolf watches the sky first and finds it “divinely beautiful… also divinely heartless” — immeasurable resources spent on something with nothing to do with human profit. Then she looks down at the rose, which has been standing still and steady in the earth all afternoon while nobody watched.

Specimen — the comfort

> It is in their indifference that they are comforting.

Virginia Woolf, *On Being Ill*, The Hogarth Press, 1930.

Not that the flowers care. That they do not, and are therefore not asking anything of you. Nothing in that garden requires you to be upright, on time, or getting better. It is the one relation in the essay with no demand in it — and Woolf finds it, characteristically, at the exact moment she has stopped being able to stand up.

Queering Earth Sheet No. 1 Accessioned 7 Sep 2026

# Coming to Terms

https://queering.earth/coming-to-terms
The readings · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/)

Sheet · an essay

# Coming to Terms

**Written by**
: Ryan Boren

**Written**
: 25 September 2022

**First published**
: [Stimpunks Foundation](https://stimpunks.org/2022/09/25/autigender-and-neuroqueer-two-words-on-the-relationship-between-autism-and-gender-that-fit-me/)

**This text**
: The essay as published, with the quotations from other writers taken out. Ryan’s words are unchanged. A treatment on labels — copias, smorgasbords, and who does the applying — was appended below it in September 2026.

**Appended**
: 8 September 2026

**Terms**
: [Autigender](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/autigender/) · [Neuroqueer](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuroqueer/)

A kid in Southern Baptist Texas in the 1970s and 80s has no vocabulary for what he is, only a steady refusal of rules that strike him as senseless. The one bit of colour he risks — a pink tint on a new pair of glasses — his father has removed. Decades later, two words fit: autigender and neuroqueer. This sheet mounts the essay he published in 2022, his words unchanged and under a heading taken from his own sentence, and then takes up what it stops short of: what a word that fits is *for*, and what it charges.

## Against My Grind

I didn’t have the vocabulary for what I felt back in Southern Baptist Texas in the 1970s and 80s, but I was uncomfortable with and resistant to gender norms as a kid. They felt: silly, arbitrary, oppressive, confining, unnecessary, counter-productive, irrational. They did not make sense. They did not fit.

A small, shareable anecdote of the ways norms went against my grind, from a lifetime collection:

I didn’t openly express myself in dress much—I was deathly afraid of being noticed and totally unsure about what I felt—but I would splash some color in. I opted for a pink tinted coating on a new pair of eyeglasses once. Kids at school gave me grief, but I liked them and came to wear them as a defiant badge and also a sort of shield. My father had the coating removed.

![A hand-coloured lithograph of two orchid blooms. Broad tawny sepals and petals, heavily freckled with dark red, spread around a frilled lip of deep pink and magenta with a yellow throat. Thick green leaves and pale roots sit below.](images/floral-magazine-1870-plate-511.jpg)

Plate 511, [*The Floral Magazine*, volume 9](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/50241086) (London: L. Reeve & Co., 1870). Drawn and lithographed by Worthington G. Smith; printed by Vincent Brooks, Day & Son. Public domain, digitised by the [Biodiversity Heritage Library](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/).

Several burnouts and a retirement later, I have zero capacity for masking, for attenuating myself to the sensibilities of surrounding bigots and bullies. I enjoy my pink and my flower print Thai fisherman pants and wistfully wishing I could dial my gender to my pansexual, polyamorous, genderpunk, genderqueer mood.

[Autigender](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/autigender/) and [neuroqueer](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuroqueer/) are the best fits I’ve found after a lifetime of seeking. Perhaps a term that fits even better will emerge. Perhaps it’s already out there for me to discover. I’ll keep reading other queer Autistics as we help each other figure ourselves out.

Appended four years later

The section above — *Against My Grind* — is the essay of 25 September 2022, Ryan’s words unchanged. **Its heading is his own phrase**, lifted from the anecdote inside it; the lede at the head of the sheet is ours. What follows was written for this sheet in September 2026, because the account above stops at the moment two words fitted and says nothing about what a word that fits is *for*, or what it charges. **Every quotation below was read in the work it comes from** and is logged in the site’s [attribution ledger](https://queering.earth/ledger). Most of it was gathered first from the [Stimpunks glossary](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/labels/) and the [gender copia page](https://stimpunks.org/gender/copia/), where Ryan has been collecting these quotations for years. **Each one names the copy it was read in**, which is the part that matters: the Jack passages come from a scan of the printed article, and the print punctuates her differently from the digital text — the [register](https://queering.earth/changelog) has that. One line is a transcription of speech and says so.

## A copia, not a category

The case against labels nearly always assumes a label is a box — a container, sized in advance by somebody else, that a person is put inside and does not get out of. Against that picture, of course labels look like cages, and of course the humane-sounding move is to ask for fewer of them.

But look again at what the words in that last paragraph are doing. *Pansexual, polyamorous, genderpunk, genderqueer*, and then *autigender* and *neuroqueer*: six words in two sentences, not one of them a box, not one of them cancelling any of the others. That is not a classification. It is a **copia**.

*Copia* is a rhetorician’s word for abundance. Erasmus wrote two books on it — [*De duplici copia verborum ac rerum*](https://archive.org/details/derasroterodamid00eras), on the twofold abundance of words and of matter — on the principle that you cannot choose the expression that lands until you have generated the whole range to choose from. The abundance is not ornament. It is the method, and its proper name is invention.

**Jordynn Jack pointed that word at gender.** Reading autobiographies, blogs, and forum posts by Autistic writers, she found something that would not sit on either of the models on offer:

Specimen — the copia

> The sources considered here imply not a binary model (masculine/feminine) or even a view of gender as a continuum, but something more like a *copia*, the rhetorical term Erasmus used to describe the practice of selecting “certain expressions and mak\[ing\] as many variations of them as possible” (17). *Copia* provides a strategy of invention, a rhetorical term for the process of generating ideas. To be specific, *copia* involves proliferation, multiplying possibilities so as to locate the range of persuasive options available to a rhetor.

Jordynn Jack, [“Gender Copia: Feminist Rhetorical Perspectives on an Autistic Concept of Sex/Gender”](https://doi.org/10.1080/07491409.2012.667519), *Women’s Studies in Communication* 35:1 (2012), 1–17, at p. 3, **read in a scan of the printed article**. Her “(17)” is a page reference to Erasmus, *On Copia of Words and Ideas*, edited by Donald King and David Rix (Milwaukee: Marquette University Press, 1963), which is the edition her works-cited list names. **Jack writes *autistic* in lower case throughout**, and her sentences are not restyled to this site’s house capitals.

**A strategy of invention** — that is the phrase to hold on to. Copia is not a rack of labels waiting to be issued. Invention, in rhetoric, is the generating stage, the part before the choosing, and Erasmus’s book is two books for that reason: one on abundance of words, one on abundance of matter. Abundance is the method, not the mess.

And a copia is something you can see the extent of. Jack lists what her writers were reaching into — “*genderqueer, transgendered, femme, butch, boi, neutrois, androgyne, bi-* or *tri-gender, third gender*, and even *geek*”, and then, because gender does not arrive by itself, “terms related to sexuality, such as *straight, gay, lesbian, pansexual, bisexual*, and so on.” Set that beside the two sentences above it and the overlap is not a coincidence: *pansexual* and *genderqueer* are on both lists, and the whole point of the second one is that it does not stop where the first one does.

Her conclusion is the sentence this sheet is built on. What the diversity of her sources supports, she writes, is “an expanded concept of autistic gender identity that pushes past a gender continuum toward a copia, in which terms can be tried on and appropriated, discarded, and invented while still being understood as embodied and constructed.” **Tried on, appropriated, discarded, invented** — four verbs, all of them things a person does, none of them things done to a person.

Specimen — the buffet

> Language is not a set menu, it’s a buffet.

The Leftist Cooks, [*Spider-Verse, Identity Politics, Leftist Infighting, and the Oppression Olympics*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_WcBJNHcrHs), YouTube, 20 August 2023. **A spoken line, and the transcription is ours** — taken down by Ryan Boren watching the video and published on the [Stimpunks glossary](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/labels/). The channel and the date are confirmed from the video; the wording is his ear, and this sheet does not pretend otherwise.

Sonny Jane Wise arrived at the same shape from the other end of the room, and set a better table for it. Their *Neurodiversity Smorgasbord* borrows from the relationship smorgasbord — the idea that you describe what a relationship actually is instead of filing it under *platonic* or *romantic* — and does the same thing to neurodivergence:

Specimen — the plate

> If we’re rolling with the analogy of a smorgasbord, there are a lot of different ingredients that make up the diversity of our minds. You could say each individual is a plate of various ingredients and tasty treats. Each of us are our own unique combination of ingredients and there are infinite combinations of ingredients.

Sonny Jane Wise, [*The Neurodiversity Smorgasbord: An Alternative Framework for Understanding Differences Outside of Diagnostic Labels*](https://www.livedexperienceeducator.com/blog/theneurodiversitysmorgasbord), Lived Experience Educator, 27 September 2024.

So: a plate. You go down the line, you take what is yours, you leave what is not, and what you carry back is not a verdict on you. It is a description, assembled by you, of one particular evening. Somebody else’s plate has three of the same things on it and four you have never eaten, and neither plate is wrong, and neither is the buffet.

## The same materials, arranged differently

There is a version of this put precisely rather than culinarily. Florence Ashley’s account of gender identity begins from a problem that looks like an argument and turns out to be a floor plan:

Specimen — the building materials

> To arrive at a gender identity, we arrange gender subjectivity like building materials. My theory helps us understand how different people offer seemingly incompatible accounts of their gender identity without questioning their authenticity or validity. They simply arrange similar building materials differently.

Florence Ashley, [“What Is It like to Have a Gender Identity?”](https://doi.org/10.1093/mind/fzac071), *Mind* 132:528 (October 2023), 1053–1073, from the abstract.

Two people can hand you flatly contradictory accounts of what their gender consists of. One says it is her body. One says it is a set of preferences and a way of moving through a room. One says it is nothing she can locate at all. Ashley’s move is to stop treating that as a contradiction needing a winner. The materials overlap; the buildings do not. What differs is the arrangement, and an arrangement is not a lie.

**This is what keeps a copia from being a free-for-all.** The parts are real — the body, the messaging, how a pronoun lands when somebody uses it, what a boy did with a pair of pink-tinted glasses and what his father did about it. What is underdetermined is what you build out of them. More than one building stands up.

## Self-applied, or it is a different object entirely

All of that holds in one direction of travel only. Reverse it and every good thing about it inverts.

Specimen — the hinge

> Only when people get to choose their own labels will we get anywhere toward building an equitable culture.

Ira David Socol, [*Using “Correct Language” And “People First”*](https://web.archive.org/web/20210304193914/http://blogs.slj.com/bowllansblog/2009/05/12/using-correct-language-and-people-first-by-ira-david-socol/), guest post at Bowllan’s Blog, *School Library Journal*, 12 May 2009. Read in the Internet Archive’s capture; the original address no longer resolves.

Socol is writing about people-first language, but that sentence is the hinge the whole question turns on. **A label you reach for and a label you are handed are not the same object in different clothes.** One is invention. The other is classification, and classification runs one way: the group that gets named is the group being sorted, and everyone else gets to be the unmarked case. The word can be letter-for-letter identical — *Autistic* on a plate you assembled, *autistic* on a form somebody else filled in about you — and the two do opposite work.

Nick Walker built the direction of travel into the grammar, which is the most durable place to put it:

Specimen — the verb, then the adjective

> And, just like *queer*, the adjective form of *neuroqueer* can also serve as a label of social identity. One can neuroqueer, and one can *be* neuroqueer.

> Or, to put it more concisely (but perhaps more confusingly): you’re neuroqueer if you neuroqueer.

Nick Walker, [*Neuroqueer: An Introduction*](https://neuroqueer.com/neuroqueer-an-introduction/), neuroqueer.com — first published 2015, revised 2021. The definitive version is collected in [*Neuroqueer Heresies*](https://neuroqueer.com/neuroqueer-heresies/) (Autonomous Press, 2021).

The verb comes first and the label accrues to whoever does the thing. You are not *eligible* for it; you are *doing* it. Which is precisely why it cannot be issued to you from a desk: **nobody can diagnose you with a practice.**

## What the label buys

None of which makes the handed-down kind disposable, and this is where the argument usually goes wrong in the other direction. A word arrived at in a clinic still opens doors that no self-description opens: a support plan, a legal protection, a reasonable adjustment, an explanation that lands after thirty years of not having one. And it opens a door that has nothing to do with paperwork — other people who recognise the description. A 2023 thematic analysis of Autistic LGBTQIA+ identity and inclusion takes its title from one sentence: “My whole life has been a process of finding labels that fit.” That is the good of them, put as a life’s work rather than a slogan.

Helen Edgar, writing against a campaign to have autism and ADHD retired as “invented labels”, puts the aim where it belongs:

Specimen — the wrong object

> However, it is not labels that disable us or our children, it is the bureaucratic structure that attaches value and resources to labels rather than to authentic needs. When a child is only seen as deserving of support once labelled, the problem lies with the gatekeeping logic and finances of the institution and system, not the real identity and needs of the child.

Helen Edgar, [*Inclusion Needs Recognition, Not Erasure: A Neurodiversity-Affirming Approach*](https://autisticrealms.com/inclusion-needs-recognition-not-erasure-a-neurodiversity-affirming-approach/), Autistic Realms, 18 October 2025.

Take the word away and the gate is still there. All that has gone is the key — and the people who lose a key they were already struggling to get are not the people who were ever going to be fine either way.

## What the label charges

And still there is a bill, and it comes due in three ways. The copia hardens: a term invented to describe a *relationship* to gender turns into a type of person, and the thing that was a strategy of invention becomes another set of boxes with nicer paint. The list lengthens and does less: past a certain point each new word explains a smaller share of you and takes more work to carry. And the plate starts eating the evening — you find yourself defending the arrangement instead of living in it.

-

> Labels can become barriers when used inflexibly or in a pathologizing way.

> Labels can also be liberating when used to affirm identity, understanding, and belonging when adopting a neuro-affirming approach.

Helen Edgar, *Inclusion Needs Recognition, Not Erasure*, Autistic Realms, 18 October 2025 — two consecutive lines, and she does not choose between them.

-

> A list of words and identities doesn’t really begin to scratch the surface of my experience and it’s making me more insular than I’d like.

autisticltd, [*Shedding my labels*](https://autisticltd.co.uk/2024/03/04/shedding-my-labels/), Autistic and Living the Dream, 4 March 2024. The blog carries no personal name; the handle is the byline.

-

> I’m reveling in the shedding of labels whilst appreciating the immense privilege I have to know who I am, to have words for my experiences, and the resources to find my own.

autisticltd, *Shedding my labels*, 4 March 2024 — the last line of the post.

**Read the order of that last sentence before you borrow it.** The shedding comes first and the privilege comes second, and the privilege named is not wealth: it is *knowing who I am* and *having words for my experiences*. You can only put down what you have already picked up. Somebody who has never had a word that fits is not travelling light — they are lost, and telling them that labels are limiting is telling them to stay that way.

## Six heads on one stem

The drawing at the top of this sheet is one arching stem carrying six flower heads, and not one of them matches another. That is not a mistake in the botany. It is the argument: one life, one stem, and a marigold, a coral, a violet, a verdigris, a lichen, and a marigold again, all of them growing off the same plant at the same time and none of them the plant’s true colour.

Which is why the essay above ends where it ends, and why that ending is not modesty. “Perhaps a term that fits even better will emerge.” A copia does not close. The plate is for this evening. **A label is a description you are making, not a verdict you received** — and the test was never whether it will hold for good. It is whether, today, it fits.

[https://doi.org/10.1089/aut.2021.0074](https://doi.org/10.1089/aut.2021.0074)

Socol, I. D. (2009, May 12). *Using “correct language” and “people first.”* Bowllan’s Blog, School Library Journal. [https://web.archive.org/web/20210304193914/http://blogs.slj.com/bowllansblog/2009/05/12/using-correct-language-and-people-first-by-ira-david-socol/](https://web.archive.org/web/20210304193914/http://blogs.slj.com/bowllansblog/2009/05/12/using-correct-language-and-people-first-by-ira-david-socol/)

Walker, N. (2021). *Neuroqueer: An introduction*. neuroqueer.com. [https://neuroqueer.com/neuroqueer-an-introduction/](https://neuroqueer.com/neuroqueer-an-introduction/) (Original work published 2015)

Wise, S. J. (2024, September 27). *The neurodiversity smorgasbord: An alternative framework for understanding differences outside of diagnostic labels*. Lived Experience Educator. [https://www.livedexperienceeducator.com/blog/theneurodiversitysmorgasbord](https://www.livedexperienceeducator.com/blog/theneurodiversitysmorgasbord)

# The Die Uncast

https://queering.earth/promises-like-pie-crust
The readings · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/)

Sheet · a reading

# The Die Uncast

**Specimen**
: *Promises like Pie-crust*

**Maker**
: Christina Rossetti

**Written**
: 20 April 1861 — the date her brother read off her notebooks

**First printed**
: *New Poems* (Macmillan, 1896), edited by William Michael Rossetti — thirty-five years later, and two years after her death

**This text**
: The 1896 first printing, pages 130–131. Line 20 keeps its colon

**Read**
: 8 September 2026

**Read by**
: Ryan Boren

**Read alongside**
: Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti (2026), [*Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity*](https://doi.org/10.1177/09593535261422510)

**Terms**
: [Caves, campfires, watering holes](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/caves-campfires-watering-holes/) · [Shared-air space](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/shared-air-space/) · [Monotropism](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/monotropism/) · [Co-regulation](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/co-regulation/)

In 1861 Christina Rossetti wrote twenty-four lines refusing to promise anybody anything, and put them in a notebook. A hundred and sixty-five years later a paper in *Feminism & Psychology* gave the thing she was refusing a name — the relationship escalator — and asked what would happen if Autistic people were told, early, that stepping off it was allowed. This sheet reads the poem as the permission slip nobody handed me.

Specimen — the poem, entire

> Promise me no promises, So will I not promise you: Keep we both our liberties, Never false and never true: Let us hold the die uncast, Free to come as free to go: For I cannot know your past, And of mine what can you know?

> You, so warm, may once have been Warmer towards another one: I, so cold, may once have seen Sunlight, once have felt the sun: Who shall show us if it was Thus indeed in time of old? Fades the image from the glass, And the fortune is not told.

> If you promised, you might grieve For lost liberty again: If I promised, I believe I should fret to break the chain: Let us be the friends we were, Nothing more but nothing less: Many thrive on frugal fare Who would perish of excess.

Christina Rossetti, *Promises like Pie-crust*, written 20 April 1861. Text from the first printing in [*New Poems by Christina Rossetti, Hitherto Unpublished or Uncollected*](https://archive.org/details/newpoemshitherto00rossuoft), edited by William Michael Rossetti (New York and London: Macmillan, 1896), pages 130–131, read in two separate scanned copies of that edition. Public domain. The alternating indent is hers as printed; the spaces the compositor set before every colon are not, and are closed up here — see below.

## Promise me no promises

I read *Promises like Pie-crust* as liberation from eternal vows and possessive romance into something more compatible with my ways of being.

Look at what the first stanza actually declines. Not the other person — the *promise*. Not the closeness, but the claim. “Keep we both our liberties” is a plural: the poem is not protecting one party from the other, it is protecting the same thing in both of them, and it treats that thing as the precondition for anything else. Then it goes further and declines certainty itself: “Never false and never true.” The die is *held*, uncast. Not thrown and lost, not put away — held, in the hand, with the outcome still open.

Cisgender heterosexual monogamy has always been a bad fit for me. The poem helped me develop my solo polyamorous and pansexual identity.

## The escalator, and not knowing there was a way off

The thing Rossetti is standing beside without a name for it got named in 2026, in a paper built out of the words of forty-six Autistic adults. The authors borrow the term from Amy Gahran: the **relationship escalator**, the single moving staircase from dating to exclusivity to cohabitation to marriage to children to lifelong monogamy, on which every step both proves and demands the next.

Specimen — the false assumption

> There are a great many social normativities … and “social scripts” such as the relationship escalator, all of which are based around the false assumption that humans don’t vary.

Liriava, 53, genderqueer, pansexual, LGBTQ+ group, quoted in Monique Huysamen, Chris Hatton and Marianthi Kourti, [*Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity*](https://doi.org/10.1177/09593535261422510), *Feminism & Psychology*, 2026. The ellipsis is in the paper.

What the paper is really about is not the escalator. It is the cost of not being told there is a way off it.

Specimen — the consequences of not knowing

> Together, these narratives reveal the consequences of not knowing – and not being supported to know – about possibilities for intimate relationships beyond cisgender heterosexual monogamy.

Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, *Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity*, 2026.

Which is where a poem comes in. A twenty-four-line refusal, printed in 1896 and sitting on the shelf ever since, is one of the few places a person could have found the idea before anybody thought to teach it.

## Free to come as free to go

The totalizing expectations of traditional romantic relationships are incompatible with me. They are excessive to the point of overwhelm and burnout. I need quiet parallel existence in a shared [campfire](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/caves-campfires-watering-holes/) setting and solo recharge time in a [cave](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/caves-campfires-watering-holes/) setting by myself. I need intermittent relationships where the die is held uncast, “free to come as free to go.”

[Shared-air space](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/shared-air-space/) relationships of any sort are [intensive pattern dances](https://boren.blog/2021/04/24/the-intensive-pattern-dance-of-meatspace-relationships-patterns-sensory-overwhelm-and-solo-polyamory/) done at the terrifying tempo of synchronous, full-sensory real-time. I need daily doses of solitude and regular hibernation intervals to sustainably withstand any other human being. Only in solitude do I have the space to unfurl my patterns, un-beset by the outside, and recline into their regulated peace.

![A chromolithograph on cream paper. A woody branch crosses the plate diagonally and a slender vine is wound loosely around it in open spirals, its thin tendrils curling free at both ends. Hanging below on a green stalk is a dense cluster of pale yellow trumpet flowers with frilled, red-flushed mouths, all facing different ways. Two long brown seed pods hang above, one split open. Small pencil dissections of a flower and two seed sections sit along the bottom.](images/annales-lugduno-batavi-1863-tab5-tecoma-ceramensis.jpg)

Tab. V, *Tecoma ceramensis*, from [*Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi*](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/652159), volume 1 (Amsterdam: C. G. van der Post, 1863). Drawn by **A. Bernecker**, signed “A. Bernecker. del.” in the lower left; chromolithographed by Emrik & Binger of Haarlem, whose imprint is in the lower right. Public domain; scanned from the Missouri Botanical Garden, Peter H. Raven Library copy for the [Biodiversity Heritage Library](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/).

I need my “own rhythms and temporalities” — and that phrase is the paper’s, describing exactly this:

Specimen — counter-narratives

> These narratives resist and queer the heteronormative, neuronormative, ableist expectations of ‘the relationship escalator’, complete dependence, coliving and cosleeping as the defining features of a legitimate relationship. They offer counter-narratives following their own rhythms and temporalities, and value independence rather than framing it as a deficit.

Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, *Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity*, 2026.

**Value independence rather than framing it as a deficit.** That sentence is doing a lot of quiet work. The clinical literature has spent decades reading a preference for one’s own home, one’s own bed and one’s own schedule as social impairment. Here it is read as a relationship structure, which is what it is.

Specimen — my own home environment

> I tried sharing a home with a partner in the past, and it did not work for me. I prefer being in control of my own home environment and having a flexible schedule. I also prefer being by myself when I am not feeling well, particularly when I am not feeling well mentally.

PhotonPulse\_he\_him, 47, male, heterosexual, men’s group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

## Many thrive on frugal fare

Every line speaks to me, especially the ending:

Specimen — the last two lines

> Many thrive on frugal fare
> Who would perish of excess.

Rossetti, *Promises like Pie-crust*, 1861.

Read that as a sensory statement and it stops being a proverb about modesty. *Perish of excess* is what happens to a body given more input than it can process — more contact, more noise, more presence, more obligation to be available. Rossetti reaches for *frugal* and *excess*, words about quantity, and puts *thrive* and *perish* on either side of them. Not better and worse. Different amounts, and a different amount is fatal.

![A chromolithograph on cream paper. Two large ripe fruits, russet-orange and heavy, hang from a thin woody branch with glossy dark green leaves. Between them a third fruit is drawn cut in half in grey pencil, showing two pale seeds packed side by side inside a thick husk. Smaller pencil studies of flowers and buds run along the bottom edge.](images/annales-lugduno-batavi-1863-tab4-gonystylus-miquelianus.jpg)

Tab. IV, *Gonystylus miquelianus*, from [*Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi*](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/652124), volume 1 (Amsterdam: C. G. van der Post, 1863). Signed “van Aken et Bernecker, ad viv. del.” — two hands, drawing from the living plant; chromolithographed by Emrik & Binger of Haarlem. Public domain; scanned from the Missouri Botanical Garden, Peter H. Raven Library copy for the [Biodiversity Heritage Library](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/). Mounted here for the weight of the thing, not as an argument.

This is the same move Woolf makes on [the first sheet on this plate](https://queering.earth/on-being-ill): a claim that reads as temperament turns out, on inspection, to be a claim about a body.

## Keep we both our liberties

I need time to immerse myself in my [monotropic](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/monotropism/) interests. My interests are a relationship in themselves. I immerse myself in them and get into flow states that are necessary to maintain regulation and mental health. “Keep we both our liberties” so that I may pursue my passions.

Let us [co-regulate](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/co-regulation/) together, and let us regulate apart pursuing our passions.

Darwin drew the thing itself, without meaning to. A tendril of white bryony, caught on a twig at one end and held by its own stem at the other, contracts into a spiral — and the spiral runs *one way* from one end and *the other way* from the other, with a short straight stretch in the middle where the two turns meet. He printed it as [Fig. 13](https://archive.org/details/cu31924024538922/page/n178) of *The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants*, captioned “A caught tendril of *Bryonia dioica*, spirally contracted in reversed directions”, and it is worth going to look at.

One attachment, holding. Two ends, each turning its own way. **The straight bit in the middle is where neither one gave in.** Darwin is explaining a mechanical necessity — a tendril fixed at both ends cannot coil in a single direction without unwinding itself — and reading it as a diagram of anything else is entirely our doing. But it is the best picture of “keep we both our liberties” that anybody has drawn, and its author thought he was describing a weed.

Specimen — there are concepts for this

> There are concepts such as Living Apart Together and solo polyamory which address the idea that relationships must include cosleeping and cohabitation.

Liriava, 53, genderqueer, pansexual, LGBTQ+ group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

The definition of the second of those that I keep coming back to is Amanda Van Slyke’s, and it turns on ownership rather than on logistics:

Specimen — solo polyamory

> Solo polyamory is the idea that people are autonomous beings who have different needs and wants, and alongside good communication and mutual respect between all partners, no one puts rules on each other because no one owns one another.

Amanda Van Slyke, [How Polyamory Helped Me Advocate For My Needs As A Disabled Person](https://thought.is/how-polyamory-helped-me-advocate-for-my-needs-as-a-disabled-person/), Thought.is.

*No one owns one another.* Rossetti gets there in the negative, a hundred and sixty years earlier, by declining to hand over the deed.

## Not alone in needing to be alone

I’m not alone in my need to be, sometimes, alone. I’m not alone in my need for multiple different people with different ways of being to fill my life when it needs filling, to co-regulate me when I need to be with someone in a meaningful way to help balance and recharge the sensory system and bodymind.

![A hand-coloured plate on grey paper showing two groups of small mushrooms. The upper group is six pale cream ones, including two tiny unopened buttons; the lower group is seven brown-capped ones. In both groups every specimen stands on its own tuft of earth, at a different size, angle and stage of opening, with clear space between each one and the next.](images/cooke-1881-british-fungi-plate-85.jpg)

Plate 85 from Mordecai Cubitt Cooke, [*Illustrations of British Fungi (Hymenomycetes)*](https://archive.org/details/illustrationsofb01cookuoft), volume 1 (London: Williams and Norgate, 1881–91). Two species on one plate: *A* is *Agaricus (Lepiota) sistratus*, “in Gardens”; *B* is *Agaricus (Lepiota) mesomorphus*, “in woods. New Forest.” Signed **M.C.C.** in the lower-left corner — Cooke’s own initials; his preface says the contributors’ initials are attached to their drawings. Public domain; scanned from the University of Toronto copy for the [Biodiversity Heritage Library](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/).

One plate, two species, and not one specimen on it touching another. Every one at its own size, its own angle, its own stage of opening, on its own tuft of earth — one group found in gardens, the other in the New Forest, and arranged together on one sheet anyway.

The paper’s participants over fifty say the not-knowing out loud, and it is the hardest part of it to read.

Specimen — the nearest easiest offers

> At the ripe age of 67, I can honestly say I wished I had followed less conventional relationships. With two failed heterosexual marriages (three kids all following pretty straight stuff) and a non-live-in 7 year partnership I feel like I missed out on aspects of love and intimacy just by responding to the nearest easiest offers.

Indigo\_Regent\_She\_Her, 67, female, pansexual, mixed group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

Specimen — never taught this was an option

> I often think that if I had known polyamory was a thing when I was younger I would have chosen to form relationships in this way, but I was never taught this was an option or how to navigate these types of relationships.

MerryFennel, 39, female, bisexual, women’s group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

Specimen — more than one way of doing it

> I struggled in my early 20s when I first tried to date in a neurotypical way and follow conventions, I did not know that there was more than one way of doing it.

NeuroGator, 50, nonbinary, lesbian, LGBTQ+ group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026.

Three people, three decades apart, saying the same sentence: nobody told me. Not *I chose wrong*. *I did not know there was a choice.*

## Let us neuroqueer relationships

Let us [neuroqueer](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuroqueer/) relationships so that they suit our authentic ways of being instead of forcing us to live in falsity.

![A chromolithograph on cream paper. A large pale yellow five-petalled flower opens at the top over a cluster of green and pink buds. Below it, three leaves of the same plant are painted three different colours: one deep matte green, one glossy russet-brown, and one pale grey-green seen from beneath. A small red-and-cream flower and a row of pencil dissections sit along the bottom.](images/annales-lugduno-batavi-1863-tab9-wormia-subsessilis.jpg)

Tab. IX, *Wormia subsessilis* Miq., from [*Annales Musei Botanici Lugduno-Batavi*](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/652299), volume 1 (Amsterdam: C. G. van der Post, 1863). Signed “Th. Rocke, del.” in the lower left; chromolithographed by Emrik & Binger of Haarlem. Public domain; scanned from the Missouri Botanical Garden, Peter H. Raven Library copy for the [Biodiversity Heritage Library](https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/).

Look at the leaves on that one plant. Green, russet, and a pale underside — painted as three different things because at the moment somebody sat down in front of it, they *were* three different things. A plate that averaged them into one correct leaf would be a worse record of the plant.

That is close to where the paper lands, and the paper lands there as a demand on services rather than as a hope:

Specimen — a neuroqueer ethic

> …good social care and support for intimate lives is underpinned by a neuroqueer ethic, one which affirms difference and divergence from the norm and supports autistic people to build intimate lives in their own time and in ways that are pleasurable, safe, and affirming to them.

Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, *Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity*, 2026. The sentence begins “These findings show that, ultimately, good social care…”; the opening is elided here and the lower-case *g* kept.

Specimen — on their own terms

> Good support, they contended, entails helping autistic people realise this, while actively supporting them to navigate and build intimate relationships on their own terms.

Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, *Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity*, 2026.

Specimen — shifting the course

> …becoming aware of, and being supported to safely explore, alternative ways of doing relationships opens choices and avenues with the potential to shift the course of people’s intimate lives.

Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, *Embrace Difference, Challenge Normativity*, 2026. The sentence begins “This research shows that becoming aware of…”.

One thing worth saying about how that evidence was gathered, because the method is the argument too. The five focus groups were **asynchronous and text-based**, run on a forum over six weeks by an Autistic researcher, with participants anonymous to each other and free to arrive, leave and return at their own pace. The authors chose it deliberately, to make “space for alternative temporalities”. A study about people who need their own rhythms was built to run on them. Nobody had to sit in a circle and take turns at somebody else’s tempo in order to say that sitting in a circle at somebody else’s tempo does not work for them.

## A colon, where everyone else prints a full stop

Now the reason this sheet names its printing on the label.

In the 1896 first printing, the poem’s lines end in colons. Eight of the twenty-four do, and there are exactly **two full stops in the whole poem** — at line 16, closing the second stanza, and at line 24, closing the poem. The text in general circulation, including the copy at the [Poetry Archive](https://poetryarchive.org/poem/promises-pie-crust/), has three. The extra one lands here:

Line 20, as printed

| 1896, *New Poems*, page 131 | The text now in circulation |
| --- | --- |
| I should fret to break the chain* :* | I should fret to break the chain*.* |

A full stop there closes “If you promised, you might grieve … I should fret to break the chain.” into a finished sentence, and makes “Let us be the friends we were” a fresh proposal that follows it. The colon does something else: it makes the whole stanza one movement, in which the friendship is not a new offer but *the consequence* of everything said before the mark. *Because* a promise would cost you your liberty and cost me my peace — so let us be the friends we were.

And the line that acquired the extra full stop is the line about breaking the chain.

**The colon is not one library’s smudge.** It was read twice, in two separately scanned copies of the 1896 edition — the Princeton one and [Victoria University’s in Toronto](https://archive.org/details/newpoemshitherto00rossuoft) — and the mark, the alternating indent and the date line all agree. The Princeton pages were rendered as images and read rather than trusted to a text extractor, because a finding about one punctuation mark is not something an extractor is evidence about.

**Two things this sheet is not claiming.** It is not claiming Rossetti’s manuscript, which we have not seen. Her brother printed from the seventeen notebooks she left, and he vouches in his preface for the accuracy of the *dates* in them; he says nothing about her punctuation, and he left no note on this poem at all. The colon is the earliest reading we can actually put our eyes on, not a certified one. Nor is it claiming that somebody deliberately changed the mark: a full stop in place of a colon at the end of a quatrain is the most ordinary silent tidying there is, and it may have happened in a schoolbook in 1930 and been copied ever since.

What it claims is narrower and it holds: **the earliest printing has a colon, the copies you will find have a full stop, and a sheet that quotes one while dating it to the other has said something untrue.** [The Woolf sheet](https://queering.earth/on-being-ill) is here for the same reason, in reverse — there the tidy commas turned out to be the author’s own earlier version, and the untidy *and…and…and* her later one. The lesson is not “trust the older text.” It is: name the printing, or do not quote.

Two smaller things about the 1896 page, so that a reader who goes and looks is not confused. The first word of the poem is set as “PROMISE” after a large drop-cap *P*, which is how the volume opens every poem; the word is *Promise*. And the compositor set a space before every colon, semicolon and question mark, all through the book — that is the house style of the volume, not Rossetti’s pointing, so the spaces are closed up above. The title over the poem is in full capitals, again for every poem; the volume’s own contents page gives it as *Promises like Pie-crust*, which is the form this sheet uses. Modern editions mostly print it *Promises Like Pie-Crust*.

## What this sheet will not tidy

**Rossetti was not writing this.** She wrote twenty-four lines in April 1861 to a “you” the printing does not name, and her brother, who dated the poem and published it, left no note saying who or why. She had no relationship escalator to step off, no word for what I am, and no reason on earth to be proposing an arrangement. Reading her refusal forward until it arrives at solo polyamory is *our* move, and it is the whole method of this site rather than a discovery about her. The language is hers. The use is mine.

**And the poem’s own bargain is not the one I am describing.** “Let us be the friends we were, nothing more but nothing less” keeps the liberty by giving up the intimacy. What I want, and what the paper’s participants want, is the opposite trade: keep the intimacy, several of them, and give up the ownership. Rossetti hands back the whole thing. I am borrowing her terms for a deal she did not offer.

**The title is borrowed too, and we cannot say from whom.** “Promises and pie-crust are made to be broken” was already proverbial when she used it. The attribution in circulation runs to Jonathan Swift’s *Polite Conversation* of 1738, which we have not read in a primary, and there are recorded uses earlier still. So this sheet names no owner for the saying rather than repeating one it has not checked.

**And Darwin’s tendril has a second half to it that the sheet has so far left out.** Darwin says, on the same page, that the reversed spiral “never occurs with uncaught tendrils; and when this appears to have occurred, it will be found that the tendril had originally seized some object and had afterwards been torn free.” A coil is evidence of a hold. A coil on something holding nothing is evidence of a hold that ended. Nothing in the poem, and nothing on this sheet, makes that costless — a life of coming and going leaves a shape behind either way, and “free to go” and “torn free” are not the same event described twice.

**Independence is not automatically a happy ending, and the paper does not pretend it is.** Set against every quotation above, from the same study, is this one:

Specimen — growing old alone

> Thinking about what life would look like, I hate sharing a bed to sleep in but not many people are up for considering living separately or in separate rooms. I like my space. I like my independence (although need social care support daily to facilitate that). I think I get a lot of what I need in life from friendships (even with a limited number of people) I do worry about growing old alone though.

Vero, 32, female, queer, LGBTQ+ group, quoted in Huysamen, Hatton and Kourti, 2026. Her punctuation.

The authors do not resolve that, and neither will this sheet. Vero is not failing to want independence. She wants it, has it, needs paid support to have it, and is frightened by what it may cost her in forty years — because the people around her are still on the escalator, and a life off it is much lonelier than it needs to be when almost nobody else has been told they were allowed to step off. **The scarcity is the problem, not the preference.** That is an argument for more people knowing sooner, which is exactly what the paper asks for, and it is the argument a poem from 1861 has been quietly making from the shelf the whole time.

Let us hold the die uncast.

Queering Earth Sheet No. 3 Accessioned 8 Sep 2026

[Label corrected four times](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-08-rossetti) on mounting, then [corrected once more and re-determined twice](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-08-plates) when the plates changed.
