# Wyrd, Weird, and the Invention of Normal

https://queering.earth/invention-of-normal
The readings · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/)

Sheet · a reading

# Wyrd, Weird, and the Invention of Normal

**Specimen**
: [*Wyrd, Weird, and the Invention of Normal*](https://morerealms.com/becoming-weird-wyrd-normality/)

**Maker**
: [Helen Edgar](https://morerealms.com/)

**First published**
: More Realms, July 2026

**This text**
: Helen’s essay, her outline, and her reading list, read out into a sheet. Her published sentences are quoted and linked wherever they appear. The argument is hers; the sentences around her quotations are ours, and this label is where we say so.

**Read**
: 8 September 2026

**Read by**
: Ryan Boren

**Terms**
: [Weird](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/weird/) · [Normal](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/normal/) · [Neuronormativity](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuronormativity/) · [Ethodiversity](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/ethodiversity/) · [Autistic Joy](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/autistic-joy/)

There is a demotion inside the word *weird*. It began as wyrd — Old English for fate, for the thing that has power over you — and it ended up as the thing that is wrong with you. This sheet follows the drop, and asks who was standing at the bottom of it holding the new definition.

Before it meant strange,

it meant fate.

1.

wyrd

Old English

Fate; that which comes to pass. Built on weorþan, to become. Kin to weorþ, the ancestor of *worth*. A force you answer to.

2.

weird

c. 1400 onward

Having power to control fate — and then, by way of three women on a Scottish heath and an eighteenth-century stage, uncanny. A quality you carry.

3.

weird

From about 1820

Odd-looking, strange, disturbingly different. A deviation you are corrected for. Set here in the institution’s own typeface, because by this point the institution is the one saying it.

The dates are from the [Online Etymology Dictionary](https://www.etymonline.com/word/weird), which puts the sense “odd-looking, strange, disturbingly different” at 1820. Everything above that third slip is more than a thousand years long. The sense that most people now think *is* the word is about two centuries old, and it arrived at almost exactly the same moment as *normal* did. That coincidence is the argument of this sheet.

## A force you answer to

Helen opens her essay at the root:

Specimen — the older fate

> In Old English, *wyrd* meant fate, but not necessarily the fixed, predetermined fate the word often suggests today.

Helen Edgar, [*Wyrd, Weird, and the Invention of Normal*](https://morerealms.com/becoming-weird-wyrd-normality/), More Realms, July 2026.

Not fixed, because the verb underneath it is a verb of motion. Wyrd is formed on weorþan, to come to pass, to become. And the same Germanic root gives weorþ, which becomes modern English *worth*. Alby Stone, whose short book on the subject has been in print in one form or another since 1989, puts the three senses together in one line:

Specimen — worth, death, and what will come

> Old English wyrd combines all the qualities found in the names of the three nornir: it means ‘worth’; ‘death’; and that which will happen or come to be.

Alby Stone, *Wyrd: Fate and Destiny in North European Paganism*, corrected edition (Loughborough: Heart of Albion Press, 2022), p. 37. First published 1989.

Worth and death and becoming, held in one syllable. Not a sentence handed down, but a running account of what a life has come to be worth by the end of it. Stone is blunt that the popular picture is the wrong one: what the sources actually describe, he writes, is “something much more flexible and worthwhile than the rigid, impersonal and implacable force that fate is commonly expected to be.”

The Old English poets did use it the hard way too. The Exeter Book’s *Wanderer* ends its opening sentence on a half-line that has been carried into English a hundred different ways:

Specimen — the half-line

> wyrd bið ful ārǣd

> Fate is wholly fixed — or wholly decreed, or wholly inexorable, depending on whose English you read it in.

*The Wanderer*, line 5b, Exeter Book, tenth century. Old English as printed in [Bright’s Anglo-Saxon Reader](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bright%27s_Anglo-Saxon_Reader/The_Wanderer). The English line is ours, and it is a gloss rather than a translation: ārǣd is exactly the word translators cannot agree on.

Hold both. Wyrd was heavy. It was the thing you did not get to argue with, and an Anglo-Saxon audience would not have heard anything cosy in it. **That is the point of the reclamation, not an obstacle to it.** The word did not start out as a compliment and get insulted. It started out as a *power*, and it was demoted into a defect.

## Three at the well

Where does a power like that live? In the Norse telling, at the foot of the world tree, in the hands of three women with a bucket. The *Poetic Edda* introduces them in six lines:

Specimen — Völuspá 20

> Þaðan koma meyiar, margs vitandi,þriár, ór þeim sal, er und þolli stendr;Urð héto eina, aðra Verðandi,—skaro á skíði— Skuld ina þriðio;þær lǫg lǫgðo, þær líf kuroalda bǫrnum, ørlǫg seggia.

> Thence come the maidens mighty in wisdom,Three from the dwelling down ’neath the tree;Urth is one named, Verthandi the next, —On the wood they scored, — and Skuld the third.Laws they made there, and life allottedTo the sons of men, and set their fates.

*Völuspá*, stanza 20. Old Norse after Gustav Neckel’s 1914 edition; English from Henry Adams Bellows, *The Poetic Edda* (New York: The American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1923). Both texts as set out at [Mimisbrunnr.info](https://www.mimisbrunnr.info/cv-st-19-21).

Popular retellings hand the three of them out as past, present, and future, and Helen is right to say the names suggest something more interesting than a timeline. Urð is what has come to pass. Verðandi is the present participle of verða — to happen, to become — the same verb that wyrd descends from. Skuld is debt: what is owed, what falls due. Stone reads the trio as an accounting of worth rather than a clock, and the last word of the stanza, ørlǫg, is not “fate” in the sense of a script but something closer to *that which is of the law* — the particular conditions under which one particular life has to be lived.

So the middle sister is a verb in the continuous tense. She is not the present moment. She is *becoming*, ongoing, unfinished, still being carved. If you were going to build an idea of a person on any of the three, that is the one to build it on.

## Four hands on the same three women

The word survived into Scots as a plain, unremarkable term for the Fates, and it is in Scottish chronicle that Macbeth meets them. Then four different people get hold of the same encounter over four hundred and thirty-five years, and each one leaves fingerprints:

-

> …either the weird sisters, that is (as ye would say) the goddesses of destinie, or else some nymphs or feiries, indued with knowledge of prophesie by their necromanticall science…

Raphael Holinshed, *Chronicles*, 1587 (1808 reprint, p. 269), transcribed in Bek-Pedersen (2022), p. 64.

-

> The weyward Sisters, hand in hand,
> Posters of the Sea and Land,

Shakespeare, *Macbeth* I.iii, First Folio, 1623. The Folio never prints *weird*: it prints *weyward* and, later in the play, *weyard*, six times in all. Text from the Furness Variorum via Bek-Pedersen (2022), p. 73.

-

> This word, in general, signifies perverse, froward, moody, obstinate, intractable etc. and is everywhere so used by our Shakespeare

Lewis Theobald on *wayward*, *The Works of William Shakespeare*, volume 5 (London, 1733), p. 392 — explaining why he was replacing it with *weird*. Quoted in Bek-Pedersen (2022), p. 73.

-

> Theobald may in one sense revert the picture back to the Scottish tradition of the ‘weird sisters’ by substituting ‘weyward’ with ‘weird’, but in doing so he bypasses Shakespeare altogether.

Karen Bek-Pedersen, [*Scottish Studies* 39 (2022)](https://doi.org/10.2218/ss.v39.7159), p. 76.

Read the four slips in order and you can watch it happen. Holinshed cannot decide what the three of them are — goddesses, or nymphs, or fairies, or necromancers — and reaches for all four at once. Shakespeare, writing during the witch trials, for a king who had written a book on witchcraft, resolves the confusion by making them witches and calling them *weyward*: perverse, self-willed, contrary. Theobald, a hundred and ten years later, decides that must have been a copyist’s error and puts *weird* back. And the Weird Sisters that everybody knows — the ones with the cauldron, the ones in every school edition — are Theobald’s.

**Which is a complication for the reclamation, and this sheet is not going to smooth it out.** Bek-Pedersen’s conclusion is that Shakespeare wrote witches on purpose and that Theobald misread him. If she is right, then reclaiming the Weird Sisters as figures of fate is reclaiming an editor’s Shakespeare rather than Shakespeare’s. That is worth saying out loud, because the alternative is a nice story with a footnote quietly removed from it. It also does not damage the argument much: the drift from fate to wickedness to oddness happened whoever spelled what. The interesting thing is not that one editor got it wrong. It is that *weyward* and *weird* could be confused for each other at all — that self-willed and fated were already close enough on the page to swap places.

## That which does not belong

Mark Fisher, writing about the weird as a mode rather than a genre, gives it a definition that does not mention strangeness of appearance at all:

Specimen — the definition

> …the weird is that which does not belong. The weird brings to the familiar something which ordinarily lies beyond it, and which cannot be reconciled with the “homely” (even as its negation).

Mark Fisher, *The Weird and the Eerie* (London: Repeater Books, 2016), introduction. Quoted from the ebook, which carries no page numbers.

That is a relation, not a property. Nothing is weird by itself; a thing is weird *with respect to a frame*, and the frame is somebody’s. Which means the sentence “you are weird” is always, on inspection, the sentence “you are outside the arrangement I was expecting” — and it says at least as much about the arrangement as about you.

![A rocky shore under a grey storm sky. A woman in a deep teal-blue dress stands with her back mostly to us on the pebbles, long red hair streaming sideways in the wind, one hand raised to hold it clear of her face as she watches the sea. Out to the left a three-masted ship is going over in heavy green-white breakers. Dark cliffs close the scene on the right; a broken spar and small pink flowers lie among the stones in the foreground.](images/waterhouse-1916-miranda-the-tempest.jpg)

John William Waterhouse (1849–1917), [*Miranda — The Tempest*](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Miranda_-_The_Tempest_JWW.jpg), 1916. Oil on canvas, 100.4 × 137.8 cm; private collection. Public domain — Waterhouse died in 1917 — scan via Wikimedia Commons. **Chosen by Helen Edgar.** When Ferdinand washes up, Miranda’s own count of him is “the third man that e’er I saw” — she has no average to hold a newcomer against. In the last act she gets the line about the brave new world, and she means it.

Fisher goes further, and this is the part the neurodiversity movement has been living inside for thirty years without necessarily citing him for it. The feeling of wrongness that the weird produces, he writes, “is often a sign that we are in the presence of the new. The weird here is a signal that the concepts and frameworks which we have previously employed are now obsolete.” The discomfort is data. It is the frame reporting its own limits.

## The child they said was swapped

There is an older and much worse version of being read as not-belonging, and it is worth putting on the same sheet as the Weird Sisters, because it comes out of the same fairy country.

![A night woodland in deep blue-green. A barefoot young woman with loose red hair and a circlet of small blue flowers stands among the trees in a long amber-gold dress, bending forward and gathering her skirt in both hands to look down. Around her feet a dense crowd of small winged fairies holds up glowing lanterns made of shells, seed pods and flowers, throwing warm points of light across the grass. A dark lantern lies fallen and unlit on the ground at the lower left.](images/hughes-1908-midsummer-eve.jpg)

Edward Robert Hughes (1851–1914), [*Midsummer Eve*](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Midsummer_Eve_-_Edward_Robert_Hughes_(1908).jpg), c. 1908. Watercolour with gouache, 114.3 × 76.2 cm; private collection. Public domain — Hughes died in 1914 — scan via Wikimedia Commons. **Chosen by Helen Edgar.** Her lantern is out. Theirs are lit, and there are more of them.

Across Northern Europe, when a child did not develop the way a family expected, one available explanation was that the child had been taken and something else left in the cradle. Susan Schoon Eberly, working in a hospital developmental disabilities department, went through the fairy literature and read it as a body of folk diagnosis: changeling stories, she argues, are the folk record of children born with conditions that had no other name. Her article is called [*Fairies and the Folklore of Disability: Changelings, Hybrids and the Solitary Fairy*](https://doi.org/10.1080/0015587X.1988.9716425), and it is not a charming read. The remedies attached to changeling belief were exposure, immersion, beating, and fire. In March 1895, at Ballyvadlea in County Tipperary, Bridget Cleary was burned at her own hearth by her husband, who had spent days insisting that the woman in the house was not his wife but a changeling. Nine people were charged over her death. He was convicted of manslaughter.

**So: no romanticising the fae on this sheet.** Being called a changeling was not a compliment about your interesting inner life. It was the first draft of “this child is wrong,” and it had a body count.

What the same tradition also holds, though, is the other half of the story — the one where somebody refuses to let go. In the Scots ballad of Tam Lin, Janet is told exactly what the fairy host will do to the man she is trying to get back. They will change him in her arms, over and over, into things designed to make her drop him:

> ‘They’ll turn me in your arms, lady, Into an esk and adder; But hold me fast, and fear me not, I am your bairn’s father.

> ‘They’ll turn me to a bear sae grim, And then a lion bold; But hold me fast, and fear me not, As ye shall love your child.

> ‘Again they’ll turn me in your arms To a red het gaud of airn; But hold me fast, and fear me not, I’ll do to you nae harm.

*Tam Lin*, stanzas 31–33 of version A, from Francis James Child, *The English and Scottish Popular Ballads* (Boston, 1882–98), ballad 39. *Esk* is a newt; a *red het gaud of airn* is a red-hot bar of iron.

*Hold me fast, and fear me not.* Three times, once per transformation, and the instruction never changes. The ballad is completely clear that the shapes are not the problem — the shapes are a test of whether the person holding on will keep holding on. Janet does not fix him, and she is not asked to. She is asked to stay, through the adder and the bear and the bar of iron, and to know the whole time that the thing in her arms is the person she came for.

Set beside a hundred years of therapy aimed at making a child hold still, that is a startling piece of advice to find in a ballad. It is also, more or less exactly, what every Autistic adult writing about meltdown says they needed and did not get.

And the other half of the fae bargain, the one where the child is glad to go, is the poem everybody knows:

> Come away, O human child! To the waters and the wild With a faery, hand in hand, For the world’s more full of weeping than you can understand.

W. B. Yeats, [‘The Stolen Child’](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Wanderings_of_Oisin_and_Other_Poems/The_Stolen_Child), from *The Wanderings of Oisin and Other Poems* (1889). In the last stanza the refrain turns around: “For he comes, the human child, / To the waters and the wild… / From a world more full of weeping than he can understand.”

Yeats knew what he was doing with that switch. Three times it is an invitation; the fourth time it is a report, and the child has gone. Read it as a poem about leaving a world that will not have you and it is unbearable. Read it as a poem about finding the other people who are also leaving, and it is the founding document of every weird scene there has ever been.

## Refusal is not a no

Which brings up the thing that gets called withdrawal, or non-compliance, or refusal to engage, and is usually none of those.

Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang, building on Audra Simpson’s account of the Kahnawà:ke Mohawk community declining to be made legible to anthropology, argue that a refusal is not an absence. It is a position:

Specimen — a generative form

> Refusal is not just a “no,” but a redirection to ideas otherwise unacknowledged or unquestioned.

Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang, “R-Words: Refusing Research”, in Django Paris and Maisha T. Winn (eds), *Humanizing Research: Decolonizing Qualitative Inquiry with Youth and Communities* (Thousand Oaks: Sage, 2014), p. 239. They are drawing on Audra Simpson, “On Ethnographic Refusal: Indigeneity, ‘Voice’ and Colonial Citizenship”, *Junctures* 9 (2007), 67–80.

Two pages later they put it flatly: “refusal is not a prohibition but a generative form.” A refusal sets a limit on what the powerful get to know, and a methodology of refusal treats that limit “as productive, as indeed a good thing.”

**The transposition here is ours, and it needs saying plainly.** Tuck and Yang are writing about settler colonialism, Indigenous sovereignty, and the research apparatus, and their argument is grounded in that and not offered as a general theory of saying no. Lifting it onto [masking](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/masking/) is a move we are making, not one they made. What survives the move is the structure: that declining to render yourself legible on somebody else’s terms is a stance with content, and that the demand for legibility was never neutral. The unmasked Autistic person who stops performing fluency is not failing to communicate. They are declining a translation, and the translation was always in one direction.

## Joy is not a coping strategy

The other thing that gets misread as a symptom is delight.

Elliot Wassell’s study of Autistic joy put a questionnaire to eighty-six Autistic people, most of them women, girls, or non-binary, asking whether they experience joy and what it is made of. Sixty-seven per cent said they often do; ninety-four per cent said they actively enjoy aspects of being Autistic. The paper’s finding is not that Autistic people cope well. It is that the joy is native, and the obstacle is other people.

-

> …the key barrier to joyful experience is not autism itself but other people’s lack of acceptance of authentic autistic behaviours such as stimming and pursuit of special interests.

Elliot Wassell, [“Experiences of autistic joy”](https://doi.org/10.1080/09687599.2025.2498417), *Disability & Society* 41:1 (2026), 236–261, from the abstract.

-

> No matter how ‘weird’, ‘age inappropriate’, or ‘useless’ our passions might seem to them, for us, this is what makes life worth living.

Participant 28, quoted in Wassell (2026), p. 249.

-

> Queercrip joy is more than finding new happy objects—it is refusing to collapse ‘positive’ affects and ‘negative’ affects into a mutually exclusive binary.

Megan Ingram and Kai Jacobsen, [“Both because of and in spite of: Towards the reclamation of queercrip joy”](https://doi.org/10.1177/13634607241264319), *Sexualities* 28:3 (2025), 795–810, at p. 804.

Note where Participant 28 puts the scare quotes. Not around *passions*. Around *weird* — the word arriving from outside, in somebody else’s voice, to be held at arm’s length while the sentence carries on.

Ingram and Jacobsen supply the guard rail that stops any of this becoming a slogan. Queercrip joy, they argue, exists *both because of and in spite of* pain: it is not the opposite of suffering, not a replacement for it, and not evidence that everything is fine. Joy and grief are simultaneous and co-constitutive, and a joy that has to pretend otherwise is just cheerfulness with a quota. That is the difference between celebrating [Autistic joy](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/autistic-joy/) and using it to change the subject.

## Where the whimsy gets policed out

None of this is subtle in practice. There is a whole apparatus for training play, [stimming](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/stimming/), and delight out of people, and most of us went through it before we were ten.

odd difficult immature too much attention-seeking non-compliant weird

Those are the words, and behind them is [behaviourism](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/behaviorism/) in the classroom, [deficit ideology](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/deficit-ideology/) in the paperwork, and professionalism at work — the last of which is mostly a dress code for affect, requiring legible seriousness at all times and reading enthusiasm as a lapse. The Stimpunks glossary has the structural name for the whole arrangement: [neuronormativity](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuronormativity/), a set of norms and expectations that centre one way of functioning as the right way, then treat everything else as a disorder. Wassell’s participants describe its effects in one line each. Less pressure to always be doing. Not being forced to mask so long we lose touch with ourselves.

## Where it gets let back in

The counter-image is not a slogan either; it is a set of rooms. Stimpunks builds and describes them: [caves, campfires, and watering holes](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/caves-campfires-watering-holes/) as the three spatial modes a mixed group of humans actually needs, and [Cavendish Space](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/cavendish-space/) as the name for a place designed around monotropic attention and sensory reality instead of around compliance. The Campfire Learn Together sessions are the working example — including [the one on the mycelial worldview](https://stimpunks.org/2026/07/08/campfire-learn-together-the-mycelial-worldview-is-punk/), which is about fungi and is therefore about distributed intelligence with no commanding centre, decomposition as a form of care, and mischief as a method.

What all of those spaces have in common is that nobody in them is managing your weirdness. That is the entire specification. Everything else — the lighting, the seating, the option to leave — follows from it.

## Normal is younger than the railways

Here is the part that reframes everything above. Wyrd is more than a thousand years old. *Normal*, as a thing a person can be, is about two hundred.

Robert Chapman’s *Empire of Normality* tells the story through Adolphe Quetelet, a Belgian astronomer who turned the statistical tools built for tracking stars onto human beings, and published *l’homme moyen* — the average man — in 1835. Quetelet did not stop at describing the average. He recommended it:

Specimen — the type of perfection

> If the average man were completely determined… we might consider him as the type of perfection; and everything differing from his proportions or condition, would constitute… a monstrosity.

Adolphe Quetelet, quoted in Robert Chapman, *Empire of Normality: Neurodiversity and Capitalism* (London: Pluto Press, 2023), chapter 2. Chapman’s sentence carries the quotation in three pieces, broken by “he wrote” and “he went on”; the ellipses here mark those breaks and nothing else.

Chapman’s own line on what happened next is the one to keep:

Specimen — a mistake of nature

> The error curve developed to predict the course of stars now applied to human normativity, and to be abnormal was to be a mistake of nature.

Robert Chapman, *Empire of Normality* (London: Pluto Press, 2023), chapter 2, “The invention of normality”. Quoted from the ebook, which carries no page numbers.

The word for a deviation, in the mathematics Quetelet borrowed, was *error*. It meant a measurement that had missed the star. Transferred onto people, with the average recast as the ideal, it meant a person who had missed being right. And Chapman’s larger argument is that this was not a discovery that happened to have consequences: the Empire of Normality is “an apparatus of material relations, social practices, scientific research programmes, bureaucratic mechanisms, economic compulsions, and administrative procedures,” and it tightens the acceptable range because a system organised around productivity has a use for a narrow one.

Set the two clocks side by side, which is Helen’s move and the best sentence in her essay:

Specimen — the exchange

> Somewhere along the way, worth got redefined as fitting in, while being different stopped being something we valued at all.

Helen Edgar, [*Wyrd, Weird, and the Invention of Normal*](https://morerealms.com/becoming-weird-wyrd-normality/), More Realms, July 2026.

That is the whole demotion in one sentence, and it is exact. Weorþ and wyrd came from the same root: worth was what a life turned out to be, measured at the end, in its own terms. The bell curve replaced that with worth as proximity to a mean — measurable at any moment, against everybody else, in somebody else’s units.

## Wider than neuro

One more frame, because [neuronormativity](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuronormativity/) is not the only normativity in the room and the neurodiversity paradigm is not the widest available lens.

Ombre Tarragnat proposes [ethodiversity](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/ethodiversity/) — “short for ethological diversity,” referring to “the intra- and inter-specific variabilities and differences in behavioural or existential styles in (human and nonhuman) animals”. The term, Tarragnat writes, “parallels ‘biodiversity’ and ‘neurodiversity’”, and contains neurodiversity without being limited to it: it takes in the somatic and the behavioural as well as the neurological, and it learns from the range of ways animals are.

Which is a paradigm with room in it for whimsy. Not whimsy as a therapeutic technique or a wellbeing intervention or a strength to be leveraged, but as one existential style among many — no more in need of a justification than a heron’s way of standing in a river. Chapman notes in passing that neuroqueering, in Nick Walker and Remi Yergeau’s sense, “focuses on embracing weird potentials within one’s neurocognitive space”. Weird potentials. The word is doing its oldest job in that phrase: not *defective*, and not even *strange*, but *what this life might still turn out to be*.

## What this sheet will not tidy

Three things, left standing.

**An etymology is not an argument.** That wyrd once meant fate does not make weirdness good, any more than the Latin in *disability* settles anything about Disabled people. Words drift; that is what words do. The reason to tell this particular drift is not that the old meaning was true and the new one is false. It is that the new one arrived on a specific date, in specific company, doing a specific job — and a meaning with a birth certificate can be argued with in a way that a timeless fact cannot.

**The Weird Sisters were probably witches.** See the wall above. The best scholarship on the question says Shakespeare wrote *weyward* and meant it, and that the Fates were put back into the play by an editor in 1733. Anyone reclaiming those three women as figures of fate is reclaiming Theobald’s text. It is still a good reclamation. It is not the one the First Folio supports.

**Nobody chooses to be read as weird.** Weird Pride is a reclamation, and reclamations are for people who already carry the word whether they want it or not. The people who can put weirdness on and take it off again are not the ones the word costs anything. [Weirdwashing](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/weirdwashing/) is the failure mode: the aesthetic of deviance, adopted by an institution that will still send the same child out of the same room.

## Still taking shape

Helen ends her essay by putting worth back where she found it:

Specimen — the close

> I think this is what wyrd actually means, human worth that was never about being static, never about being plotted somewhere along someone else’s bell curve, but about always moving, always still taking shape.

> Let’s embrace our wyrd, weirdness, and everyone else’s too.

Helen Edgar, [*Wyrd, Weird, and the Invention of Normal*](https://morerealms.com/becoming-weird-wyrd-normality/), More Realms, July 2026.

The middle sister is the one holding the bucket. Not what has come to pass, and not what is owed — the one whose name is a verb still running. Verðandi: becoming. A life is not a point on a distribution. It is a thing being carved, in the present participle, and nobody has finished reading it yet.

Find out more about [Weird Pride](https://weirdpride.day/), which falls on 4 March, and which Helen observes in July on the grounds that every day is one.

Queering Earth Sheet No. 4 Accessioned 8 Sep 2026

Provenance Mounted [8 September 2026](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-08-wyrd). [Label corrected four times and re-determined once](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-08-wyrd) — the byline first, and on Helen Edgar’s own word.

# Miranda: To Be Wondered With

https://queering.earth/the-tempest
The readings · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/)

Sheet · a reading

# Miranda: To Be Wondered With

On Shakespeare’s *The Tempest*, Waterhouse’s 1916 canvas, and who a story lets be difficult. Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren neuroqueer the play by reading it this way.

**Specimen**
: William Shakespeare, *The Tempest*

**Maker**
: William Shakespeare (1564–1616)

**First performed**
: 1611. First printed in the First Folio, 1623

**This text**
: The play, the editorial history of one speech in it, and John William Waterhouse’s 1916 canvas, read together. The quotations are the play’s and the editors’; the sentences around them are ours, and this label is where we say so.

**Read**
: 8 September 2026

**Read by**
: [Helen Edgar](https://morerealms.com/) and Ryan Boren

**Terms**
: [Neuronormativity](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuronormativity/) · [Masking](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/masking/) · [Normal](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/normal/) · [Shared-air space](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/shared-air-space/)

1. Shakespeare, 1611
2. a boy actor, 1611
3. Theobald, 1733
4. Waterhouse, 1916
5. Huxley, 1932
6. Helen & Ryan, 2026

![A rocky shore under a grey storm sky. A woman in a deep teal-blue dress stands with her back mostly to us on the pebbles, long red hair streaming sideways in the wind, one hand raised to hold it clear of her face as she watches the sea. Out to the left a three-masted ship is going over in heavy green-white breakers. Dark cliffs close the scene on the right; a broken spar and small pink flowers lie among the stones in the foreground.](images/waterhouse-1916-miranda-the-tempest.jpg)

John William Waterhouse (1849–1917). [*Miranda – The Tempest*](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Miranda_-_The_Tempest_JWW.jpg), 1916, oil on canvas. Painted the year before Waterhouse’s death, forty-one years after his first, gentler Miranda of 1875. Public domain.

Her face is turned away from us. One hand is pressed to her heart. Behind her a ship is coming apart on the rocks in cold, storm-grey light, and Waterhouse gives us none of Miranda’s expression to tell us how to feel about it, only the shape of a body absorbing someone else’s disaster as though it were happening inside her own chest. It is, art historians agree, the most emotionally exposed of his two attempts at her (DailyArt Magazine, n.d.). It is also, we want to argue, exactly the pose the play keeps putting her in: turned from us, feeling everything, granted almost none of the words that would let her account for what she feels.

Miranda’s name is Shakespeare’s own coinage, the first recorded use of it as a person’s name in English (Wikipedia contributors, n.d.). He built it from the Latin gerundive of *mirari*, to wonder at: *miranda*, she who is to be wondered at, worthy of admiration. It is a lovely name and a loaded one, because wonder runs both ways. To wonder at something can mean to marvel at it with your whole, undivided attention. It can also mean to make of a person a spectacle: something looked at, remarked upon, held up as a curiosity, never quite the one doing the looking. This reading takes Shakespeare’s word and turns one preposition: not wondered at, which the play already does to her constantly, but wondered with, the way she herself wonders with the drowning sailors before anyone tells her to. We follow Miranda through all three, because the play cannot decide between them either, and because that argument, staged on one small island four hundred years before anyone invented the statistically normal person, is still the argument this whole project keeps having.

## Assembled, not born

Before any of that, one fact underneath the whole play. When The Tempest was first staged in 1611, Miranda would not have been played by a woman. English theatre would not permit that for another fifty years. She would have been played by a boy player, part of a company apprenticeship system in which performers of female roles were, on the surviving evidence, teenagers rather than children, commonly in their mid-to-late teens, cast for frame and voice and drilled in the gait, gesture, and vocal register that stood in for femininity on that stage (Kathman, 2005). Her modesty, her wonder, her compliant softness: every trait the play offers as Miranda’s nature was, at the moment of its first performance, a rehearsed construction laid onto a body the role needed nobody in the audience to think twice about.

This is not a trivia footnote. It is Judith Butler’s argument about gender arriving three hundred and eighty years early and without ever citing Shakespeare: identity is not an interior truth that gesture and costume merely express, but “a stylized repetition of acts,” a performative accomplishment that both the audience and the performer come to believe in the doing of it (Butler, 1990). There was never a natural woman underneath Miranda for the boy actor to reveal. There was only the performance, repeated eight times a week until it read as nature. Waterhouse restages her in oil in 1916. This sheet restages her again in 2026. Nobody in this whole four-hundred-year chain ever got to meet an un-staged Miranda, including, arguably, Miranda.

## A household of three

Prospero was put to sea with his daughter when she was three years old, and for twelve years afterward their whole society is an island the size of a single household: a father, a daughter, and Caliban, with Ariel felt everywhere and seen by no one but Prospero. Miranda grows up with almost no comparison class. She has never seen a woman other than her own reflection, by her own account, and no man but her father, until Ferdinand. In the vocabulary Stimpunks’ own glossary uses, this is a [shared-air space](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/shared-air-space/) (Stimpunks Foundation, n.d.): physical, co-located presence, three bodies breathing the same weather for twelve years, rather than the digitally networked togetherness the term was coined to stand alongside. Twelve years on an island with three people is the household Miranda knows, and it is the only one she has ever had the chance to learn.

None of this should read as an argument that isolation was secretly a gift. Alison Kafer’s work on crip time is useful precisely because it refuses to romanticise a slower or smaller world on principle, and instead keeps asking who gets to set its pace and shape (Kafer, 2013). Miranda did not choose the island and could not have left it. Prospero controlled the only boat, the only magic, and, for twelve years, the only company. Describing her household is not the same as approving of it, and the play never actually lets her answer that question on her own terms.

The play, and four centuries of criticism after it, mostly cannot see this as anything but a wound waiting to be corrected by re-entry into the wider world. That correction has a name by the end of Act 5. We want to sit with the household of three a little longer before the crowd arrives.

## O, I have suffered with those that I saw suffer

The very first thing Miranda does on stage, before Prospero has told her anything, before she knows the wrecked men are staged, before she knows her own history, is feel the shipwreck in her body as though it were happening to her.

Specimen — Act 1, Scene 2

> If by your art, my dearest father, you havePut the wild waters in this roar, allay them.… O, I have sufferedWith those that I saw suffer: a brave vessel,Who had, no doubt, some noble creature in her,Dash’d all to pieces.

*The Tempest*, Act 1, Scene 2 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

She has not been asked to imagine their suffering. She has not calculated, from social cues, that suffering is the appropriate response. She simply reports it as a fact about her own body: I have suffered with those that I saw suffer. It is a strange verb tense for a play that has not shown her the wreck happening more than a moment before, and it reads less like sympathy performed for an audience than like attunement that runs ahead of explanation, feeling arriving before the story that would justify it. Waterhouse’s canvas, four hundred years later, paints exactly this line and nothing else: not Miranda deciding to care, but Miranda already, wordlessly, mid-suffering.

## Be collected. No more amazement.

And then, within a dozen lines, her father tells her to stop.

Specimen — Act 1, Scene 2

> Be collected.No more amazement. Tell your piteous heartThere’s no harm done.

*The Tempest*, Act 1, Scene 2 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

This is not comfort so much as instruction. Prospero does not ask what she feels; he specifies what she is now permitted to feel, and issues it as a command in the imperative mood, before he has explained a single thing that would actually justify the reassurance. It is the same regulatory gesture the masque scene will later perform on her body, staged here first on her interior state: an outside authority deciding the correct amount and duration of someone else’s feeling. Reading this as an autistic reader might recognise it immediately, because it is the shape of every “you’re fine” delivered to a person who is, from the inside, plainly not being asked what fine would mean to them. [Neuronormativity](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuronormativity/) does not only police what a body does. It polices what a body is allowed to still be feeling once the socially appropriate window for feeling it has closed.

## Abhorred slave

A few dozen lines later Miranda is given, in the First Folio of 1623, the hardest speech in the scene. Here is what four centuries of editing did to it.

<del>PROSPERO</del><ins>Miranda, First Folio, 1623</ins>

> Abhorred slave,Which any print of goodness wilt not take,Being capable of all ill! I pitied thee,Took pains to make thee speak, taught thee each hourOne thing or other…

Reassigned to Prospero by editor Lewis Theobald, 1733, restored to Miranda in the Folger edition and others since (Folger Shakespeare Library, n.d.; Shakespeare Navigators, n.d.).

It is a speech of real authority: an accusation, a claim to have been Caliban’s teacher, a judgment about who deserves what. Theobald moved it to Prospero’s mouth on the reasoning that it did not seem credible that a girl, taught language herself as a small child on the island, could plausibly have been the one who taught Caliban to speak (Shakespeare Navigators, n.d.). Many editions followed him for the better part of three centuries. The strikethrough above is not decoration. It is the actual editorial history: a name crossed out and a different name written over it, silently, in edition after edition, until it needed a restoration to notice it had happened at all.

Notice what that eighteenth-century edit actually does. It is not a correction of a printing error; it is a decision about which register of speech a young woman is allowed to hold. Compassion, wonder, suffering-with: those stay hers without dispute. Judgment, command, the claim to have been someone’s teacher and to be entitled to be angry about the return on that labour: those get quietly reassigned to her father, because an editor two hundred years ago found her difficulty, her spikiness, less credible coming from her than from him. It is the same reflex this collection has already traced at the level of a whole language, the nineteenth-century invention of the statistically normal person against which everyone else became a deviation (Edgar, 2026). Here it happens a century earlier, at the level of a single attribution line in a single scene: whose hardness gets to be plausible, and whose has to be softened into someone else’s.

It is also not an isolated case. Ann Thompson’s survey of Shakespeare’s editorial history finds the same reflex recurring across the canon, editors softening, reglossing, or reassigning a woman character’s harder or more sexually frank lines whenever those lines strained what the editor thought she should plausibly say. Adriana’s self-accusation in The Comedy of Errors has been glossed by more than one editor as her belatedly admitting a fault she never actually confesses to. The Quarto Othello’s more physically frank Desdemona was set aside by editors reaching for the Folio’s softer wording instead (Thompson, 2001). Theobald moving Miranda’s hardest speech into her father’s mouth is not one eccentric decision. It is a single instance of a pattern with a three-hundred-year paper trail, editors deciding, play after play, which register of speech a woman is allowed to be caught using.

## Before all sanctimonious ceremonies

Miranda’s courtship is not something that happens to her so much as something staged around her. Prospero engineers the shipwreck, times Ferdinand’s arrival, watches the two of them fall in love from a distance he has arranged, and later, at the betrothal masque, delivers a warning to his future son-in-law about his daughter’s body that Miranda is not recorded as hearing:

Specimen — Act 4, Scene 1

> If thou dost break her virgin-knot beforeAll sanctimonious ceremonies mayWith full and holy rite be minister’d…

*The Tempest*, Act 4, Scene 1 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

This is heteronormativity staged as literal stagecraft: a father choreographing, timing, and finally verbally contracting his daughter’s marriage and its sexual terms, with magic standing in for all the ordinary social machinery that does the same work off an island. Caliban’s own line about Miranda, spoken earlier in the same scene of the play, makes plain what the stakes of that policing actually were:

Specimen — Act 1, Scene 2

> O ho, O ho! would’t had been done!Thou didst prevent me; I had peopled elseThis isle with Calibans.

*The Tempest*, Act 1, Scene 2 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

Miranda’s safety, in other words, was never secured by her own consent. It was secured by Prospero’s control of Caliban’s body, just as her marriage is secured by Prospero’s control of the entire scene Ferdinand walks into. Postcolonial readings of the play have long noted that Miranda’s own kindness toward Caliban, teaching him language, trying to civilise rather than simply subjugate him, is not an escape from her father’s colonial logic but a softer version of it: the missionary rather than the whip, aimed at the same outcome (see, broadly, the postcolonial critical tradition summarised in Lie, n.d.). We do not want to resolve that into either condemnation or credit. We want to leave it exactly as uncomfortable as it is: gentleness is not automatically outside empire’s reach.

## I’ll die your maid

And yet inside all that staging, Miranda does something the plot did not strictly require of her. She proposes.

Specimen — Act 3, Scene 1

> I am your wife, if you will marry me;If not, I’ll die your maid: to be your fellowYou may deny me; but I’ll be your servant,Whether you will or no.

*The Tempest*, Act 3, Scene 1 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

Read this against the boy actor and Butler’s stylized repetition of acts, and the moment gets sharper. Normative courtship in Miranda’s period had its own choreography of delay, indirection, and coyness, a script she has had no occasion to rehearse, because the only society available to rehearse it in was a household of three. What the scene reads as her innocence may be better read as a failure to perform the expected femininity correctly, and a failure that, instead of shaming her, becomes its own kind of honesty. She asks first. She names the terms herself. This is not a woman gracefully declining to know the rules. It is a directness the normative script has no room for, arriving anyway because nobody successfully installed the script in the first place. The scholar Jessica Slights has made a related case against reading Miranda as simply obedient and pliant, arguing that a girl raised entirely outside conventional courtship norms has no particular reason to have absorbed them, and that her willingness to ask first reads as a kind of independence her upbringing made possible rather than prevented (Slights, 2001). Both readings can be true at once. A person can be staged within someone else’s normativity and still, inside that staging, refuse to perform it correctly.

## O, brave new world

By Act 5, Miranda has spent twelve years in a household of three. Then Prospero’s magic delivers a dozen strangers onto the same small stage, and she says the line the whole play has been saving for her:

Specimen — Act 5, Scene 1

> O, wonder!How many goodly creatures are there here!How beauteous mankind is! O brave new world,That has such people in’t!

*The Tempest*, Act 5, Scene 1 (Shakespeare, 1611/2004)

Prospero’s reply is four words long and does not share her wonder: “’Tis new to thee.” He knows, and the audience knows, that the goodly creatures in front of her include the brother who usurped him and the men who set them both adrift. The wider world being sold to Miranda as liberation is not new or brave at all; it is the same court politics that exiled her in the first place, now standing on her island in wet clothes. Sara Ahmed’s account of orientation is useful here: a body raised inside one small, particular arrangement of the world is not neutral before a bigger one, it has already been shaped by what it was given to reach toward, and a “new world” can bring a body up short exactly where that body was never built to fit (Ahmed, 2006). Miranda’s wonder is the sound of that arrival. It is not evidence that the wider world was actually the better one. Three centuries later Aldous Huxley took Miranda’s line, unedited and entirely straight-faced, as the title for a novel about a civilisation engineered for frictionless normality, and gave the same words, with the same devastating irony, to his own outsider character on first meeting that world (Huxley, 1932). The line has been doing this exact work for four hundred years: naming the gap between the crowded, normal world normativity promises and the narrower, stranger, more honestly peopled world it is actually asking you to trade away.

Nothing in the text tells us whether Miranda’s household of three was worth less than the brave new world she is about to enter. It only tells us that nobody thought to ask her which she would have chosen. Nobody asked before the shipwreck. Nobody asked before the masque. Nobody asked before Theobald moved her hardest speech into her father’s mouth. Wonder, in the end, is the one register the play always lets her keep. It is worth noticing how much of everything else got quietly kept from her instead.

What this reading will not tidy

- The Folio attribution of “Abhorred slave” to Miranda is the choice this sheet leans on, but it is a live editorial crux, not a settled fact; readers should hold the Theobald tradition in view rather than treat the Folio as simply correct.
- Reading Miranda’s education of Caliban as a “softer” colonialism is a critique of her kindness, not a defence of Prospero’s cruelty by comparison. Neither is offered here as the more forgivable option.
- Wonder is not evidence of freedom. A person can be genuinely delighted by a new world and still have had no say in whether they were delivered into it.
- We are the latest people to stage her. Nothing here is a neutral account of what the play “really” means; it is Helen and Ryan doing, deliberately and on the record, the thing the chain below has always been doing.
- This reading is built from a canonical, largely English, largely male lineage: Shakespeare, an Eton-educated novelist, a Royal Academy painter, and now two more writers. Neuroqueer theory’s own roots lie mostly outside that lineage, in mad studies and disability justice traditions that owe it little. Naming that we are one more link in this particular chain is not the same as having answered why this chain, rather than another, is the one worth extending.

Restaged by

1. Shakespeare, 1611
2. a boy actor, 1611
3. Theobald, 1733
4. Waterhouse, 1916
5. Huxley, 1932
6. Helen & Ryan, 2026
7. you, reading this

Every entry in that chain believed it was the one finally looking at Miranda clearly. This is not an exemption from that pattern. It is a piece of neuroqueering, done on purpose, by two named people, in the sense Nick Walker gives the word: not a property the play or its heroine possesses, but a practice we are choosing to perform on it (Walker, 2021). The next person who restages her gets to do the same.
