# The Swell and the Dwell

https://queering.earth/wild-nights
The readings · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/)

Sheet · a reading

# The Swell and the Dwell

**Specimen**
: *Wild nights – Wild nights!* — Fr269, J249

**Maker**
: Emily Dickinson

**Written**
: About late 1861, in Fascicle 11

**Manuscript**
: Houghton Library, Harvard University — *Poems: Packet VIII, Fascicle 11*, MS Am 1118.3 (38b), one leaf in ink. Mounted below

**First printed**
: *Poems by Emily Dickinson, Second Series* (Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1891), Book II — Love, poem VII, page 97, edited by T. W. Higginson and Mabel Loomis Todd

**This text**
: R. W. Franklin’s reading of the manuscript, as published in the [Emily Dickinson Archive](https://www.edickinson.org/). The line division after “moor –” is the manuscript’s own and Franklin records it

**Read**
: 8 September 2026

**Read by**
: Ryan Boren

**Reply in verse**
: Ryan Boren. Punctuation set for print; the words and the line breaks are his

**Terms**
: [Co-regulation](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/co-regulation/) · [Safe space](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/safe-space/) · [Belonging](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/belonging/) · [Bodymind](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/bodymind/) · [Somatic](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/somatic/) · [Stimming](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/stimming/) · [Glimmers](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/glimmers/) · [Limerence](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/limerence/)

Emily Dickinson wrote twelve lines asking for one night in harbour, and there is not a single indicative verb in them. Thirty years later her first editors printed the poem — one of them apologising for it in a letter as he did — and eight of her nine dashes did not survive the trip to the press. This sheet reads it as a description of [co-regulation](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/co-regulation/) — the swell and the dwell of relational tides — and answers it in verse.

Specimen — the poem, entire

> Wild nights – Wild nights! Were I with thee Wild nights should be Our luxury!

> Futile – the winds – To a Heart in port – Done with the Compass – Done with the Chart!

> Rowing in Eden – Ah – the Sea! Might I but moor – tonight – In thee!

Emily Dickinson, *Wild nights – Wild nights!*, written about late 1861 in Fascicle 11. Text as R. W. Franklin reads the manuscript, published in the [Emily Dickinson Archive](https://www.edickinson.org/) and printed identically by the [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44087/wild-nights-wild-nights-269) from Franklin’s Reading Edition (Belknap Press, 1999). Her dashes are set here as spaced en dashes; in her hand they vary in length and angle, and telling one from a flourish is the standing problem of editing her. Line 11 runs on to line 12 on the leaf itself, and the 1891 editors made that break a line break — see below.

![A single leaf of blue-ruled writing paper photographed against a pale ground, with three stab holes down the right edge where it was bound into a fascicle. Twelve lines of small, steeply slanted brown-ink handwriting sit in three groups with a clear space between each group, every line broken off by a short horizontal stroke. A pencilled cross and the numeral 2 sit alone at the top of the page. The last group runs to five written lines rather than four, and a single pen stroke is ruled underneath it like a full stop for the whole poem.](images/dickinson-1861-wild-nights-houghton-ms-am-1118-3-38b.jpg)

*Wild Nights – Wild Nights!* in Dickinson’s hand, one leaf of *Poems: Packet VIII, Fascicle 11*, written in ink about 1861. Houghton Library, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA — MS Am 1118.3 (38b); [catalogued as F269A](https://curiosity.lib.harvard.edu/emily-dickinson-archive/catalog/195-EDA0392_F269A) in the [Emily Dickinson Archive](https://www.edickinson.org/). Reproduced under the archive’s [CC BY-NC-ND 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/3.0/) licence and unaltered: the file mounted here is the one Harvard’s own image service returned at this width. **Look at the third group.** It has five written lines, not four — “Tonight –” stands alone because the leaf ran out of room, and everything that follows on this sheet follows from what two sets of editors did with that.

In reply — Ryan Boren

Erotic and cozy. Turbulent and safe. We share space that we co-make.

Passionate gratification segued to the calm [co-regulation](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/co-regulation/) that is our shared balm.

To be in [safe space](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/safe-space/) with one you adore, basking in reciprocation and mutual understanding, that is a great feeling. That is THE feeling — craved by our kind.

Dickinson captures well [the swell and the dwell of relational tides](https://starstuff.earth/the-nearest-body-zine). The swell is of sensory passion and exploration, of [bodyminds](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/bodymind/) alive and alight in luxurious abandonment. The dwell is of [belonging and legibility](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/belonging/) — where you can put down the compass and the chart and just be: accepted and understood.

In reply, continued

Oh to be human, in a deep easy rhythm, of reciprocal need, held not in tension.

[Stimmy](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/stimming/) [glimmers](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/glimmers/) [Somatic](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/somatic/) release Sensory ease Regulated peace.

Calm quiescence, Denouement after arrival, Preceded by A love-tangled spiral.

Might I but moor In your heart and your body, In your mind and your soul, Woven delightfully.

We need not our masks Nor our constructs of gender. Let’s rest the guise And be our realest [assemblage](https://morerealms.com/expanding-the-mycelial-network-of-care-autistic-community-safety-and-rhizomatic-futures/).

With the strength of [limerence](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/limerence/) that has been requited and matched, Let’s be together And let the world pass.

## Futile – the winds

Read the second stanza slowly, because it does not say what people remember it saying. **The storm does not stop.** The winds are still blowing at the end of that line exactly as hard as they were at the beginning of it. What has changed is that they have become *futile* — a word about effect, not about strength — and the thing that made them futile is a location: “To a Heart in port.”

That is co-regulation, described more than a century before there was a word for it. Not a calm temperament. Not a coping skill. A place, and company, in which the same weather stops landing.

Specimen — a safe enough person

> Co-regulation is when we complete the stress cycle with the support of a safe enough person.

> A safe enough person is a person in safe & social mode. They have deep belly breathing, expressive face, soft gaze, calm heart rate, prosodic voice, and the ability to enjoy safe touch or closeness.

Janae Elisabeth, writing as [Trauma Geek](https://medium.com/age-of-awareness/the-neuroscience-of-community-9f0a437d3a4f), *The Neuroscience of Community*. Quoted in the Stimpunks glossary entry for [co-regulation](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/co-regulation/), which is where we read it.

“Safe enough.” Not safe. Not perfect. Enough — which is the whole reason a harbour is a harbour and not a fortress, and it is why Dickinson can leave the winds in the poem. A port that required the weather to be good would not be a port.

The clinical literature has spent decades measuring the wrong half of this. It looks for the regulated individual and finds a dysregulated one, and writes that down as a property of the person rather than of the room they were in. A 2026 paper puts the correction plainly:

Specimen — not a passive backdrop

> Co-regulation distributes adaptive labour across the system rather than concentrating it within the individual. Environments are not passive backdrops to which people must adjust; they are active participants in regulatory dynamics.

Lori Hogenkamp, Dhwani Sanghavi and Heini Natri, [*Toward an Emergent Paradigm for Neurodiversity and Health*](https://doi.org/10.1177/25739581261433443), *Autism in Adulthood*, 24 March 2026. Quoted in the Stimpunks glossary entry for [co-regulation](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/co-regulation/), which is where we read it. The authors write *labor*; house style spells it *labour*, and the quotation keeps theirs.

Dickinson had already put the environment in the sentence. “Futile – the winds – / To a Heart in port” is a claim about a system with two things in it, and the second thing is doing the work.

## Done with the Compass – Done with the Chart

Here is the line the whole sheet turns on, and it is worth being precise about what a compass and a chart are *for*. They are not what you use when you know where you are. They are what you use when you do not — instruments of continuous correction, consulted and reconsulted, every heading checked against a reading and adjusted before the next one.

**That is masking, described as equipment.** Check the face. Check the volume. Check whether that was too much. Correct. Check again. It is navigation, it never stops, and it is exhausting in exactly the way that holding a bearing in unfamiliar water is exhausting.

Dickinson does not say the navigator has arrived, or that the instruments were wrong. She says they are *done with* — put down, on the table, not needed in here. Helen Edgar names the same three things from the other end, as conditions rather than as relief:

Specimen — what safety involves

> Across education, healthcare, and employment, a common thread seems to emerge that safety is not only physical or psychological. It is sensory, attentional, relational, and political.

> Safety involves being able to focus without constant interruption.

> It involves communicating without fear of misinterpretation.

> It involves participating without masking core aspects of identity.

Helen Edgar, [*Expanding the Mycelial Network of Care: Autistic Community, Safety, and Rhizomatic Futures*](https://morerealms.com/expanding-the-mycelial-network-of-care-autistic-community-safety-and-rhizomatic-futures/), More Realms.

*Communicating without fear of misinterpretation* is the chart. *Focusing without constant interruption* is the compass. And *participating without masking core aspects of identity* is the moment both of them go down on the table — which is what Ryan’s reply asks for in as many words: “We need not our masks / Nor our constructs of gender.”

This is also the difference between being included and belonging, and it is a difference the Stimpunks glossary refuses to let go of:

Specimen — more than being included

> Belonging means more than being included. It means feeling understood, accepted, and able to participate without constantly having to explain yourself, hide parts of who you are, or push past exhaustion just to keep up.

From the Stimpunks Foundation glossary entry for [belonging](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/belonging/). Read there on 8 September 2026; the entry gathers several sources and this passage carries no separate byline within it, so it is credited to the glossary rather than to a named author.

Being included is being allowed on the boat. Belonging is being done with the compass.

## Rowing in Eden

Two words, and both of them are doing work that generations of readers have mostly spent on the second one.

**Eden is before shame.** Not before sex — before the part where somebody notices they are naked and reaches for a covering. That is a sentence about masking too, in the oldest available vocabulary.

**And *rowing* is labour.** It is rhythmic, repetitive, bilateral, whole-body work; it is the least ethereal verb available for what she is describing, and she chose it over floating, over drifting, over sailing. A body doing a repeated motion in time, and the doing of it is the pleasure. There is a word for that on this site:

Specimen — an adaptive mechanism

> Autistic adults highlighted the importance of stimming as an adaptive mechanism that helps them to soothe or communicate intense emotions or thoughts and thus objected to treatment that aims to eliminate the behaviour.

Steven K. Kapp, Robyn Steward, Laura Crane, Daisy Elliott, Chris Elphick, Elizabeth Pellicano and Ginny Russell, [*‘People should be allowed to do what they like’: Autistic adults’ views and experiences of stimming*](https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361319829628), *Autism* 23:7 (2019), 1782–1792. The paper writes “autistic” in lower case; this site capitalizes **Autistic**, and the quotation keeps the authors’ usage.

Ryan’s reply puts it in a line: “Stimmy glimmers / Somatic release / Sensory ease / Regulated peace.” Four nouns, no verb, and it is the same grammar Dickinson uses in “Rowing in Eden – / Ah – the Sea!” — a state named rather than an action reported.

None of which is happening to a mind. It is happening to a [bodymind](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/bodymind/), which is Margaret Price’s term and is not a decorative compound:

Specimen — not minds riding around

> Mind is an embodied phenomenon. The mind is encoded in the brain as ever-changing webs of neural connectivity. The brain is part of the body, interconnected with the rest of the body by a vast network of nerves. The activity of the mind and body creates changes in the brain; changes in the brain affect both mind and embodiment. Mind, brain, and embodiment are intricately entwined in a single complex system. We’re not minds riding around in bodies, we’re bodyminds.

Nick Walker, interviewed by Dora M. Raymaker in [*Toward a Neuroqueer Future: An Interview with Nick Walker*](https://doi.org/10.1089/aut.2020.29014.njw), *Autism in Adulthood* 3:1 (2021), 5–10. The term is **Margaret Price’s**, from [*The Bodymind Problem and the Possibilities of Pain*](https://doi.org/10.1111/hypa.12127), *Hypatia* 30:1 (2015), 268–284, where she says she took it up out of trauma studies; Sami Schalk carries it into disability studies in *Bodyminds Reimagined* (Duke University Press, 2018). Both are quoted in the Stimpunks glossary entry for [bodymind](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/bodymind/), which is where we read all three.

**And now look at what Dickinson capitalizes.** Heart. Compass. Chart. Sea. Eden. In her hand they are proper nouns — a common noun with a capital on it is an object with a label on it, which on a herbarium sheet is the difference between a plant and a specimen. She pins the Heart and the Compass to the page as things. The 1891 editors took four of those pins out, and we will come to that.

## Might I but moor – tonight

The poem asks for **one night**.

Not a life, not a vow, not an arrangement. *Tonight.* And the word for a small bounded moment of regulation that is worth having on its own terms, without being the down payment on anything, is [glimmer](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/glimmers/) — Deb Dana’s coinage out of polyvagal work, and the opposite of a trigger:

Specimen — micro-moments

> Deb Dana first used the term glimmers to describe “micro-moments of regulation that foster feelings of well-being.”

Helen Edgar, [*Glimmers: Autistic Joy and Monotropism*](https://autisticrealms.com/glimmers-autistic-joy-and-monotropism/), Autistic Realms, quoting **Deb Dana**. Dana’s own book, *The Polyvagal Theory in Therapy* (W. W. Norton, 2018), has not been read here, so the coinage is credited to her at one remove and the quotation is Helen’s page.

Specimen — when everything aligns

> Glimmers are small but powerful moments when everything aligns; our focus, sensory needs, and emotions come together in a way that feels right. For Autistic people, these fleeting moments of joy, peace, or connection offer grounding and relief in a society that often feels overwhelming.

Helen Edgar, [*Glimmers: Autistic Joy and Monotropism*](https://autisticrealms.com/glimmers-autistic-joy-and-monotropism/), Autistic Realms. Her own extension of Dana’s term, and the one this sheet is using.

*When everything aligns.* That is a description of a night, not of a life, and the poem knows it. “Might I but moor – tonight –” asks for the alignment and asks for nothing after it.

Which is where this sheet meets [the one before it](https://queering.earth/promises-like-pie-crust). Rossetti, writing in England in April 1861 — the same year Dickinson was sewing this leaf into Fascicle 11 — declines to promise anybody anything and holds the die uncast, “free to come as free to go.” Dickinson asks for tonight. Two poems, one year, an ocean apart, and neither of them is asking to get on the escalator. One refuses the future and one does not mention it.

## Were I with thee — the poem is in the subjunctive, all the way down

Now the thing that is hiding in plain sight, and it is a fact about the grammar rather than an interpretation of the imagery. **Count the finite verbs in this poem.** There are three, and every one of them is a conditional:

- “Were I with thee” — subjunctive.
- “Wild nights should be / Our luxury” — conditional, and dependent on the line above it.
- “Might I but moor” — optative, and a question that the poem never answers.

Everything else has no finite verb at all. “Futile – the winds –” has none. “Done with the Compass –” is a participle. “Rowing in Eden –” is a participle. “Ah – the Sea!” is an exclamation with nothing in it that happens. **Nothing in this poem takes place.** Twelve lines, three verbs, no indicative — it is a poem made entirely of a mood, in both senses of the word.

And that is the strict definition of the term Ryan’s last stanza reaches for:

Specimen — the desire to be desired

> Limerence is a state of involuntary obsession with another person. The experience of limerence is different from love or lust in that it is based on the uncertainty that the person you desire, called the “limerent object” in the literature, also desires you. Since limerence is the desire to be desired, it is a cognitive, as well as physical, and emotional experience. As the focus of limerence is whether or not the object of desire reciprocates the feelings, rather than actually falling in love with the person, it is almost always one-sided.

[Limerence](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/limerence), *Psychology Today*. The word was coined by the psychologist **Dorothy Tennov** in the 1970s, in *Love and Limerence: The Experience of Being in Love* (Stein and Day, 1979), which has not been read here. Both are quoted in the Stimpunks glossary entry for [limerence](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/limerence/), which is where we read them.

**Uncertainty is not a symptom of limerence. It is the definition.** Take the uncertainty out and the word does not apply any more — which is why the poem’s grammar is the evidence for the diagnosis. A speaker who was moored would have written an indicative sentence.

So watch what the reply does with its own verbs, because it is not doing the same thing at all. It opens flat in the present indicative — “We share space / that we co-make” — borrows her subjunctive exactly once, at the centre, where it repeats “Might I but moor” back to her, and then ends somewhere she never goes: “Let’s be together / And let the world pass.” First person plural, hortative, addressed to somebody who is expected to answer.

Three moods against her one. **That is the actual distance between the two poems on this sheet**, and it is measurable in the verbs rather than argued from the feeling.

## Let us alter as little as possible

On 21 April 1891, from 25 Buckingham Street in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Thomas Wentworth Higginson wrote to his co-editor Mabel Loomis Todd about the volume they were assembling. He enclosed a preliminary selection. He wrote one sentence about editorial policy and then, immediately, a paragraph about this poem.

Specimen — Higginson to Todd, 21 April 1891

> Let us alter as little as possible, now that the public ear is opened.

> One poem only I dread a little to print—that wonderful “Wild Nights,”—lest the malignant read into it more than that virgin recluse ever dreamed of putting there. Has Miss Lavinia any shrinking about it? You will understand & pardon my solicitude. Yet what a loss to omit it! Indeed it is not to be omitted.

T. W. Higginson to Mabel Loomis Todd, 21 April 1891, printed in Millicent Todd Bingham, [*Ancestors’ Brocades: The Literary Debut of Emily Dickinson*](https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.29377) (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1945), page 127, and read there. Bingham’s own footnote to the sentence points at *Poems, Second Series*, page 97 — the page mounted in the table below. Higginson’s em dashes are closed up as printed; house style spaces them, and a quotation keeps its own pointing. “Miss Lavinia” is Lavinia Dickinson, the poet’s sister.

Read that letter as a whole and it is stranger than the famous sentence in the middle of it. Higginson is frightened of the poem, protective of a woman he is describing as a “virgin recluse” less than five years after her death, worried about what “the malignant” will see — and he prints it anyway, and the reason he gives is that leaving it out would be a loss. **He knew exactly what was in it.** The apparatus of denial and the decision to publish are in the same paragraph.

He also wrote “let us alter as little as possible” two lines earlier. Here is what reached page 97.

The manuscript reading, and *Poems, Second Series* (1891), page 97

| As Franklin reads the leaf | 1891, page 97 |
| --- | --- |
| Wild nights *–* Wild nights! | WILD nights *!* Wild nights ! |
| Futile *–* the winds *–* | Futile the winds |
| To a *H*eart in port *–* | To a *h*eart in port, — |
| Done with the *C*ompass *–* | Done with the *c*ompass*,* |
| Done with the *C*hart! | Done with the *c*hart*.* |
| Ah *–* the *S*ea! | Ah *!* the *s*ea ! |
| Might I but moor *–* tonight *–*<br>In thee! | Might I but moor<br>*To-night* in thee ! |

**Nine dashes go in and one comes out** — the em dash at the end of line 6, and even that one has acquired a comma in front of it. Four of her capitals are lowered: Heart, Compass, Chart, Sea. *Eden* keeps its capital, because *Eden* is a proper noun in anybody’s grammar and the other four were only proper nouns in hers. Three new exclamation marks and three new commas arrive. A full stop replaces the exclamation at the end of the second stanza. The poem opens with a two-line drop-cap **W**, which is how the volume opens every poem, so “WILD” is a compositor’s capital and the word is *Wild*; the same initial is why line 2 sits inset, and that indent is the drop cap rather than an editorial one. Every exclamation mark in the book has a space in front of it, which is the volume’s house style and not her pointing. And where the manuscript has a dash between the two halves of line 1, the compositor set an unusually wide space.

**The lineation is the one change that is not a tidy, and it deserves better than it usually gets.** Dickinson wrote “Might I but moor –” and ran out of leaf, so “Tonight –” went on the line below. Franklin records that division in his textual notes and reads through it: the verse line is “Might I but moor – tonight –”, and the physical break is an accident of paper. Todd and Higginson set what was in front of them. *Both are defensible.* One editor reproduced the poem and the other reproduced the leaf, and the argument between them is the whole argument about how to print Dickinson, arriving in 1891 at line 11 of this poem and never really leaving.

What is not defensible is a text that has been through both and kept neither.

## A word missing from the copy you will find

The [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/44087/wild-nights-wild-nights-269) prints Franklin, credits the edition, and gets it right. It also files the poem under *Queer Love Poems*, which is a reading rather than a fact about her, and a good one.

The [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/poem/wild-nights-wild-nights-249) prints something else. Read on 8 September 2026, poets.org gives a text that has been through the 1891 tidy and the modern restoration and come out as neither: the dashes are back, so it is not 1891; *heart*, *compass*, *chart* and *sea* are lower case, so it is not the manuscript; “Ah, the sea!” has a comma that is in no printing we have looked at; “Wild Nights” is capitalized where neither the leaf nor 1891 capitalizes it; and line 11 reads:

Line 11, as printed

| Franklin, and the leaf | poets.org, 8 September 2026 |
| --- | --- |
| Might I *but* moor – tonight – | Might I moor – Tonight – |

**The word *but* is gone**, and with it a beat of the line and most of its meaning. *Might I but moor* is a plea with a limit written into it — *if I could only*, *if I might just*, asking for the smallest possible version of the thing. *Might I moor* is a request for permission to dock. The page carries no edition, no editor and no date; it says “This poem is in the public domain,” which is true of the poem and tells you nothing about the text.

This is the third time the register has caught this shape of error, and it arrives the same way every time. [Woolf](https://queering.earth/on-being-ill) had two texts and both were hers. [Rossetti](https://queering.earth/promises-like-pie-crust) has a colon in her first printing where every circulating copy has a full stop. Here a poem that asks to be moored has had the hinge taken out of the asking. **Name the printing, or do not quote.**

One more thing, and it is about our own method rather than anybody else’s. Page 97 was read in three separately scanned copies. The first two — both digitised from University of California Libraries holdings — agree with each other and are wrong: a broken piece of type makes line 11 read *mocr* instead of *moor*, identically in both. The University of Toronto copy has the word intact. **Two scans that agree are not two witnesses if they came out of one library**, and this site had already written the lesson down once, about a scan of a Child ballad, and still nearly published a broken letter as a variant. The finding is not in the text of the poem; it is in the way we check it.

## What this sheet will not tidy

**Dickinson was not writing this.** She had no word for co-regulation, no glossary, no nervous system in the sense the term above is using, and no relationship escalator to decline. She wrote twelve lines to a “thee” the leaf does not name and sewed them into a fascicle. Reading her forward until she arrives at a regulated bodymind is *our* move, and it is the method of this whole site rather than a discovery about her. The language is hers. The use is ours.

**The speaker of this poem is not in port.** This is the hardest thing on the sheet and it undercuts most of the comfort in it, so it belongs here rather than in a footnote. The winds are futile *to a Heart in port* — and the speaker is outside, in the weather, asking to be let in. “Might I but moor” is a question the poem does not answer, in a poem with no indicative verb in it. Everything warm described above is a description of the thing this poem *wants*. The reply on this sheet is written from inside the harbour; the specimen is not.

**Limerence requited is not limerence.** “With the strength of limerence / that has been requited and matched” asks for Tennov’s intensity with Tennov’s uncertainty removed, and once the uncertainty is gone the word has stopped describing the thing. That is a deliberate turn and it is the reply’s best line, but the credit for *limerence* stays with Dorothy Tennov and the requited version is ours. **If we changed the words, they are ours** — and if we changed the meaning while keeping the word, the same rule applies.

**Helen’s assemblage runs the other way.** In her sentence the assemblages are the restrictive ones people take flight from — Deleuze and Guattari’s *lines of flight*, moving “away from restrictive assemblages”. “Be our realest assemblage” asks for one worth arriving at. The word covers both in Deleuze and Guattari, so this is an extension rather than a misuse; but hers is a sentence about escape and this is a line about arrival, and they are not the same sentence.

**We do not know who “thee” is, and this sheet is not going to guess.** The addressee is ungendered in the manuscript, the identity of Dickinson’s addressees is unsettled scholarship, and Higginson’s “virgin recluse” is evidence about Higginson. A queer reading of this poem does not need a biography to stand up, and it does not get one here. **Not knowing who she was writing to is not the same as her writing to nobody.**

**We read the facsimile and we are not setting our own readings against Franklin’s.** The leaf is mounted above and you can look at it. What is on it is a great many short strokes of varying length and angle, some of which are dashes, some of which are exclamation marks and some of which are the tail of the letter before them. Deciding which is which is the work of the two variorum editions and not of an afternoon, and it is precisely why this sheet names its edition in the label instead of claiming the manuscript.

**The facsimile is not in the public domain, and everything else mounted on this site is.** The poem is public domain. Harvard’s photograph of the leaf is offered by the Emily Dickinson Archive under CC BY-NC-ND 3.0, and we take them at their word rather than arguing about whether a photograph of a flat public-domain manuscript can carry a copyright of its own. That makes this the first plate here that is licensed rather than free, the credit line is the archive’s required one, and the file is unaltered.

**And the reply is for somebody.** It was written to a person, not to a readership, and it is mounted here at its author’s request with its punctuation set for print and nothing else touched. A sheet cannot be a private letter and a public plate at the same time. This one is both, and that is a decision rather than an oversight.

Might I but moor.

Queering Earth Sheet No. 6 Accessioned 8 Sep 2026

Provenance Mounted [8 September 2026](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-08-dickinson). [Label corrected twice and re-determined twice](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-08-dickinson) — two scans that agreed with each other and were both wrong, and a missing word.

# A Waste Garden, Flowering at Its Will

https://queering.earth/flower-codes
The readings · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/)

Sheet · a reading

# A Waste Garden, Flowering at Its Will

Violet, pansy, green carnation, and lavender were worn where they could be seen. Each was read in the end by the people it was meant to slip past, and each was picked up again afterwards by the people it had been used against.

A code you wear is a code you do not control. The whole point of a flower in a buttonhole is that it passes: it is legible to the people it is for and invisible to everyone else, and it costs nothing to put down. That is its strength for exactly as long as it lasts, and it never lasts.

These four went the same way, in the same order, a century apart from each other. A word or an object gets picked up because it is safe. It stops being safe. It becomes the name for the thing it was hiding — not a description any more but a charge, something a newspaper can print and a court can enter into evidence. And then, later, sometimes much later, the people it was used against pick it up again on purpose and wear it in the open, which is the only move left once the secret is gone.

**The flower does not change.** What changes is who is holding the meaning, and on this evidence it changes hands at least twice.

## Somebody else gathered these four

The set is not ours. Violet, pansy, green carnation, and lavender are assembled as a group by Sarah Prager in [*Four Flowering Plants That Have Been Decidedly Queered*](https://daily.jstor.org/four-flowering-plants-decidedly-queered/), JSTOR Daily, 29 January 2020, and this sheet exists because that piece put them on one table. Go and read it: it carries a good deal that is not here, including the violets sent on stage in *The Captive* in 1926, George Chauncey’s pansy craze, the Lavender Scare, and the Lavender Menace action of 1970.

**What is hers is the gathering. What is ours is the reading** — that these four are one process caught at four different moments, and that the process runs the same way each time. And one other thing is ours, further down, and it is a correction.

What this sheet quotes, and what it does not

Every quotation below was read in the work it comes from and is logged in the site’s [attribution ledger](https://queering.earth/ledger) with the date and the copy. Where a claim belongs to a scholar and we have not read the primary, the claim is named as theirs and not repeated as ours. **There is more history here than this sheet asserts**, and the gap is deliberate.

## The violet, which was a description before it was a code

![Six pale blue-violet flowers on slender stalks rising from a low clump of deeply divided leaves, the whole plant lifted on a clod of earth and photographed against a plain pale ground.](images/violet-viola-pedata-house-wild-flowers-of-new-york-1918.jpg)

Birdfoot violet, *Viola pedata*, from Homer D. House, *Wild Flowers of New York* (University of the State of New York, Albany, 1918), photographed by Walter B. Starr and Harold H. Snyder. **This is not Sappho’s violet.** It is an American species, photographed for a state museum survey twenty-five centuries later, and it is on this page because a public-domain plate of the right violet was not to hand. The plant is the genus, not the poem.

The oldest of the four is the one that was never a code to begin with. Sappho’s violets are just violets — worn, plaited, remembered — and what makes them the root of a symbol is that somebody else described her that way and the description stuck.

Specimen — the epithet

> Violet-weaving, pure, soft-smiling Sappho, I want to say something, but shame prevents me…

Alcaeus, addressing Sappho, in Henry Thornton Wharton, *Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings and a Literal Translation* (London, 1885). Wharton notes that the Greek epithet is ἰόπλοκος — violet-weaving — and that some manuscripts read ἰοπλόκαμος, *with violet locks*. The two readings are a hair apart and mean different things: one is what she does, the other is what she looks like.

Wharton, annotating a different fragment about girls plaiting garlands, records the ancient commentary matter-of-factly: “that plaiting wreaths was a sign of being in love.” That is the whole mechanism, six centuries before the common era. A thing women did with flowers was understood to mean something, by people who were not being coy about it, and it did not need to be a signal because nothing yet required it to be concealed.

**A code is what a description becomes when the description gets you into trouble.** Nothing about the violet changed between Sappho’s island and a Broadway theatre in 1926. What changed is that by 1926 it had to be a code.

## The pansy, which became the word

![A chromolithograph of eight garden pansies in yellow, mahogany, cream, and dusty rose, each with a dark blotched face, arranged with buds, leaves, a seedling, and a seed at the foot of the plate.](images/pansy-viola-tricolor-step-favourite-flowers-1896.jpg)

Pansy, *Viola tricolor* var. *maxima*, Plate 33 of Edward Step, *Favourite Flowers of Garden and Greenhouse* (Frederick Warne, 1896), plates selected and arranged by D. Bois. Digitised by the Biodiversity Heritage Library. The same genus as the violet above, bred up into a face.

The pansy is the violet’s garden cousin and it had the shortest journey of the four, because it did not stay an object. It became a word, and the word is still in use as an insult in a way that *violet* and *lavender* never quite managed.

The etymology is worth a moment, because it is the joke the language played. *Pansy* is the English of the Old French pensée — “thought, remembrance” — from penser, to think, and it arrives in English in the middle of the fifteenth century as *pense*, the flower “regarded as a symbol of thought or remembrance”. Something under five centuries later the same word is [recorded by 1929](https://www.etymonline.com/word/pansy) in its other sense, and the insult keeps the shape of the flower’s own meaning: **the charge is not what he does, it is what he is understood to have in mind.**

The 1920s and 1930s American drag scene that took the flower’s name is not ours to summarise. The historian George Chauncey is the source Prager cites for the *pansy craze*, and his *Gay New York* is where that account lives. We have not read it, so we are pointing at it rather than reporting it.

## The green carnation, which no plate can show

![Four carnations, two deep pink and two white, on long grey-green stems with narrow leaves, printed on a book page numbered 533 and captioned Carnations, Dianthus caryophyllus.](images/carnation-dianthus-birds-and-nature-1902.jpg)

Carnations, *Dianthus caryophyllus*, from *Birds and Nature* (A. W. Mumford, Chicago, 1902), page 533; digitised from the Smithsonian Institution Libraries’ copy. **These are the wrong colour and there is no right one.** A green carnation is a white carnation stood in dye. No botanical plate of the flower Wilde’s friends wore exists, because the flower they wore does not grow — which is a fair description of the code itself.

Prager writes that “the green carnation became a queer symbol in 1892 when Oscar Wilde instructed a handful of his friends to wear them on their lapels to the opening night of his comedy *Lady Windermere’s Fan*.” We have not read that back to a primary and do not assert it here as our own. What we have read is the poem, and the transcript of the morning the poem was read out in court.

Lord Alfred Douglas published *Two Loves* in *The Chameleon* in December 1894. It opens in a garden, and the garden is full of the flowers this sheet is about.

Specimen — the garden

> I dreamed I stood upon a little hill,And at my feet there lay a ground, that seemedLike a waste garden, flowering at its willWith buds and blossoms. There were pools that dreamedBlack and unruffled; there were white liliesA few, and crocuses, and violetsPurple or pale, snake-like fritillariesScarce seen for the rank grass…

Lord Alfred Douglas, *Two Loves*, first published in *The Chameleon*, December 1894. The poem ends: “I am the Love that dare not speak its name.”

**The violets are already in the poem.** Douglas is not building a code; he is describing a garden that grows what it likes, and the phrase this sheet takes its title from says so plainly — *a waste garden, flowering at its will*. Waste, in 1894, means uncultivated. Nobody arranged it. Nobody is coming to weed it.

Four months later the poem was uncultivated ground no longer. At the Old Bailey in April 1895, prosecuting counsel put the last line to Wilde as a question, and the reply is on the record in the shorthand reports.

Specimen — the same line, in court

> **Mr. Gill.** — “I daresay! There is another sonnet. What construction can be put on the line, ‘I am the love that dare not speak its name’?”

> **Witness.** — “I think the writer’s meaning is quite unambiguous. The love he alluded to was that between an elder and younger man, as between David and Jonathan; such love as Plato made the basis of his philosophy; such as was sung in the sonnets of Shakespeare and Michael Angelo; that deep spiritual affection that was as pure as it was perfect…”

*The Trial of Oscar Wilde: From the Shorthand Reports* (Paris, privately printed, 1906), pages 58–59. **His answer runs on past where we stop it**, through two more sentences about Michelangelo and Shakespeare, and the ellipsis marks that rather than any cut inside what is quoted. The report adds that Wilde spoke “with great emphasis and some signs of emotion”, and that the gallery answered with “a medley of applause and hisses” which the judge ordered suppressed.

Two small things in that exchange are worth keeping. Gill calls it a sonnet, and it is not one — *Two Loves* runs to seventy-odd lines. And the line as spoken in court reads *the love*, lower case, where the poem has *the Love*, a capitalised figure who has just given his name. The court flattened a character into a category, which is precisely what the trial did to the man in the box.

That is the turn, and it took under five months. In December the flowers are in a poem. By April the poem is an exhibit, and the buttonhole that had been a private joke among friends is a thing the newspapers can describe.

## The lavender, and the man the sentence is actually about

![Two lavender spikes in dusty violet rising above narrow grey-green leaves on a cream ground, captioned Lavender in small type at the foot of the plate.](images/lavender-lavandula-hulme-familiar-garden-flowers-1907.jpg)

Lavender, *Lavandula*, Plate 10 of *Familiar Garden Flowers*, figured by F. Edward Hulme and described by Shirley Hibberd, first series with coloured plates, 1907. Digitised by the Biodiversity Heritage Library.

One sentence carries most of the weight of lavender’s reputation, and it is quoted constantly. Prager quotes it: “One of the most notable uses of ‘lavender’ comes from the historian Carl Sandburg, who wrote in 1926 of Abraham Lincoln: ‘A streak of lavender ran through him; he had spots soft as May violets.’”

**The words are Sandburg’s, exactly. The *him* is not Lincoln.** Here is the paragraph the sentence comes from, which opens Chapter 54 on page 265 of the first volume.

Specimen — the whole paragraph

> Joshua Speed was a deep-chested man of large sockets, with broad measurement between the ears. A streak of lavender ran through him; he had spots soft as May violets. And he and Abraham Lincoln told each other their secrets about women. Lincoln too had tough physical shanks and large sockets, also a streak of lavender, and spots soft as May violets.

Carl Sandburg, *Abraham Lincoln: The Prairie Years*, volume 1 (Harcourt, Brace, 1926), page 265. Read in two independently digitised copies: the University of British Columbia Library’s copy, scanned at the University of Toronto, and an Internet Archive copy scanned at Cebu. On page 266 Sandburg says it a third time, of both of them at once — “had given these two men streaks of lavender, spots soft as May violets.”

So the celebrated sentence describes Joshua Speed, and Sandburg extends it to Lincoln in the next sentence but one, in different words, and then to the pair of them on the following page. **The substance of the claim survives the correction entirely.** Sandburg did write that of Lincoln. He did not write *that sentence* of Lincoln.

This is not a gotcha and we are not offering it as one. Prager names Speed herself in her very next sentence, and her book is partly about him; she plainly knows whose paragraph this is. What happened to the quotation is compression — the line got attached to the more famous of the two men on its way through a hundred retellings, and it arrives looking like a sentence about Lincoln because everybody has met it as one.

**That is this site’s own failure mode, and it is why we noticed.** The risk here is never an invented source; it is a true quotation whose object has quietly moved. Nothing was fabricated, no word was altered, and the citation is still correct at the level of book and author and year. Only the referent slipped, and the referent is the whole meaning: a sentence about two men in one bed in Springfield is a different sentence from a sentence about a president.

It is also, read the other way, a small demonstration of the thing this sheet is about. A phrase that meant one man is now doing service for another, because a code in circulation belongs to whoever is circulating it.

## The garden does not stay uncultivated

Line up the four and the shape is the same every time, only the interval changes.

-

violet

description → code

Plaited into garlands with nothing to hide, and still a plain description in Wharton’s notes in 1885. A signal only once there was something to signal past.

-

pansy

code → slur

The only one of the four that stopped being an object and became a word. Named for a thought, and used to name a man by what he is presumed to be thinking.

-

carnation

code → evidence

A flower that had to be dyed to mean anything, worn for two years and then read out in a courtroom. Nothing in nature to point at, which was the point.

-

lavender

code → scare → banner

The one that has been all the way round: a soft word in 1926, a purge in the 1950s, an insult meant to frighten a movement in 1969, and a slogan printed on a shirt in 1970.

The last of those is the only one of the four with a documented moment of somebody taking it back on purpose, and it belongs to the women who wore the shirts. That history is Prager’s to tell in her piece and the historians’ to tell in theirs; we have not read it to a primary and so we do not tell it here.

What we will say is the pattern, because the pattern is the reading. **A code fails by succeeding.** It works until enough people are using it, and the number of people who make it useful is the same number who make it legible from the outside. Then it is not a code any more, it is a name, and the name is in somebody else’s mouth.

And then the last move, the one that is not in the logic of codes at all: you keep wearing it anyway. Not because it hides you — it has stopped hiding anybody — but because a thing worn openly by enough people stops being an accusation and goes back to being a description. Which is where the violet started.

Douglas’s garden is the better image for it than any of the four flowers alone. Waste ground, growing what it likes, nobody’s scheme, “flowering at its will”. It is the most ordinary sentence in the poem and it is the only line in it nobody put on trial.

One thing we would like to fix and cannot from here

The right plate for the first section is a European sweet violet, *Viola odorata* — the violet of the Mediterranean, not the birdfoot violet of a New York state survey. The plate mounted above is the one we had, and the caption says so rather than letting the genus stand in silently for the species. **If you know of a public-domain *Viola odorata* plate**, it belongs here, and swapping it in is one line of markup and a caption. Say so in [the repository](https://github.com/Stimpunks/Queering-Earth/issues) and it will be.

Queering Earth Sheet No. 7 Accessioned 8 Sep 2026

Provenance Mounted [8 September 2026](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-08-flowercodes). [Re-determined once](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-08-flowercodes): the streak of lavender belongs to Joshua Speed, and only the referent moved.

# The Preferred Flower of Life

https://queering.earth/monotropa-uniflora
The readings · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/)

Sheet · a wall

# The Preferred Flower of Life

A plant that will not photosynthesise, the flower Emily Dickinson kept in her herbarium, and one Greek root shared by a 1753 binomial and a theory of Autistic attention.

**Specimen**
: *Monotropa uniflora* L. — the ghost pipe, the Indian pipe, the ghost plant

**Named**
: Carl Linnaeus, *Species Plantarum*, 1753. *Monotropa*, one turn, for the arched stem; *uniflora*, one-flowered

**Also mounted**
: Emily Dickinson to Mabel Loomis Todd, 30 September 1882 (Letter 997), and Dickinson’s poem *‘Tis whiter than an Indian pipe*, about 1879 (Fr1513A)

**Following**
: Helen Edgar, [*Monotropa Uniflora and Monotropism*](https://morerealms.com/monotropa-uniflora-and-monotropism/), More Realms, 7 July 2026 — written for the fifth anniversary of Dinah Murray’s death, and the reason this sheet exists

**Read**
: 9 September 2026

**Read by**
: Ryan Boren

**Biology**
: Not here. The mechanism — myco-heterotrophy, carbon taken from fungi and none given back — is our sibling site’s: [Star Stuff, *A Field Guide to Symbioses*](https://starstuff.earth/symbioses-field-guide.html). This sheet has the naming, the letter, the poem, and the word

**Terms**
: [Monotropism](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/monotropism/) · [Neuroqueer](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/neuroqueer/) · [Interdependence](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/interdependence/) · [Flow state](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/flow-state/)

There is a plant in the deep shade of North American, Latin American and East Asian forests that carries no green at all. It cannot photosynthesise. It does not reach for the light. It draws everything it needs from fungal threads in the soil, which draw theirs from the roots of trees — so the plant lives, entirely, on a connection nobody above ground can see. Linnaeus named it in 1753 for the single turn of its stem. Emily Dickinson pressed it into a herbarium, wrote a poem about it, and called it the preferred flower of life. Two hundred and thirty-eight years after the naming, an Autistic researcher and her neighbour reached for the same Greek root to describe a mind whose attention runs in one deep channel instead of many shallow ones.

## Seven hands on one specimen

This sheet is a **wall** rather than a reading, and the difference is not decoration. A reading has an order and an argument that arrives at the end. A wall has a chorus: many people, across two hundred and seventy years, standing in front of the same object and each seeing something the others could not. A herbarium sheet that has been in a cabinet long enough looks exactly like this — a specimen, and a stack of determination slips in different hands, every one of them signed.

-

> That without suspecting it you should send me the preferred flower of life, seems almost supernatural, and the sweet glee that I felt at meeting it, I could confide to none.

Emily Dickinson to Mabel Loomis Todd, 30 September 1882 — Letter 997, in pencil. Todd had sent her a painted panel of Indian pipes six days earlier.

-

> This limitless HyperboleEach one of us shall be -‘Tis Drama - if HypothesisIt be not Tragedy -

Emily Dickinson, *‘Tis whiter than an Indian pipe*, about 1879 — the last quatrain, from R. W. Franklin’s reading of Amherst Manuscript 483 (Fr1513A).

-

> He meant, perhaps, that the androgynous mind is resonant and porous; that it transmits emotion without impediment; that it is naturally creative, incandescent and undivided.

Virginia Woolf, *A Room of One’s Own*, chapter VI (Hogarth Press, 1929), pp. 148–149. The *he* is Coleridge, and Woolf is guessing at what he meant — twice, with a *perhaps* in each clause.

-

> Attention without feeling, I began to learn, is only a report. An openness — an empathy — was necessary if the attention was to matter.

Mary Oliver, *Our World* (Beacon Press, 2007). Transcribed by Ryan Boren from his own copy. **Not from *Upstream***, which is where this sentence is usually credited — see the label correction below.

-

> I haven’t really ever had a career, I’ve had a mission.

Dinah Murray, interviewed by Kate Fox in Dalgety Bay about a month before her death on 7 July 2021, quoted in Fox’s [tribute](https://katefoxwriter.wordpress.com/2021/08/16/tribute-to-dinah-murray/), 16 August 2021. Fox titled the poem she read at the memorial *Monotropa Uniflora*.

-

> It is a plant that refuses to be binary at the root of its being, in the same way it refuses to draw its nourishment from sunlight, the way other plants are expected to.

Helen Edgar, [*Monotropa Uniflora and Monotropism*](https://morerealms.com/monotropa-uniflora-and-monotropism/), More Realms, July 2026. *Monotropa uniflora* is a *perfect flower* in the botanical sense — stamens and pistil in one bloom.

-

> The quality of presence that the world persistently mistakes for absence, the inner life that runs deeper than it appears from the outside?

Helen Edgar, same essay, on what the *it* of Dickinson’s poem might be. Her sentence ends in a question mark and it is left here, because she is asking rather than concluding.

## One root, three turns

The Greek monotropos means turning one way. Linnaeus took it for the arched stem of a flower. Two centuries later two women in London took it for a mind. Nobody planned the rhyme, and it is not a metaphor either: it is the same word, describing the same shape twice.

1.

monotropos

Greek

Turning one way; of a single turn. Monos, one, and tropos, a turn — the same tropos that gives English *trope*, a turn of phrase.

2.

*Monotropa*

1753

Linnaeus’s genus, in *Species Plantarum*. The turn is physical: the stem arches over so the single flower hangs facing the ground. A plant named for the direction it bends.

3.

monotropism

1991 onward

Attention pooled in one deep channel rather than spread thin across many. Coined by **Dinah Murray** with her neighbour **Jeanette Buirski**, and set out in Murray, Lesser and Lawson’s 2005 paper. A turn you are, not a turn you make.

The 2005 paper is [Murray, Lesser and Lawson, *Attention, monotropism and the diagnostic criteria for autism*](https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361305051398), in *Autism* 9(2), 139–156. **Its third author is Wenn Lawson, and the journal’s byline still reads Wendy Lawson.** He is a trans man who has published under Wenn for years, and a citation that reproduces a publisher’s record over a living author’s own name is not neutral accuracy — it is a database outranking a person. We cite him as Wenn Lawson and say what the byline says, so a reader can find the paper and nobody has to be deadnamed to do it.

## Two hands, and one of them is the same hand

Mabel Loomis Todd painted a panel of Indian pipes and sent it to Emily Dickinson in September 1882. Dickinson wrote back within days, in pencil, and told her she had sent “the preferred flower of life”. Eight years later, when Todd and T. W. Higginson brought out the first posthumous *Poems*, that painting went on the cover.

**Todd is also one of the two editors who tidied Dickinson.** [Sheet No. 6](https://queering.earth/wild-nights) is about what they did to *Wild nights*: Higginson wrote “let us alter as little as possible” and then printed the poem with eight of its nine dashes gone. The hand that gave Dickinson her favourite flower is the hand that regularised her punctuation. That is not hypocrisy and it is not a scandal — it is what editing was, and Todd is the reason a great deal of Dickinson survived at all. It is simply worth saying that **the same person can be the gift and the alteration**, and that a reader who only has the tidied text cannot tell.

Gift and alteration, one hand.

## A poem, and what 1896 did to it

Three years before the letter, Dickinson had already written the plant down. The poem survives on a fragment of stationery, in pencil, about 1879.

> ‘Tis whiter than an Indian Pipe - ‘Tis dimmer than a Lace - No stature has it, like a Fog When you approach the place - Not any voice imply it here - Or intimate it there - A spirit - how doth it accost - What function hath the Air? This limitless Hyperbole Each one of us shall be - ‘Tis Drama - if Hypothesis It be not Tragedy -

Emily Dickinson, about 1879. Amherst Manuscript 483, in pencil on a fragment of stationery. Text from R. W. Franklin, *The Poems of Emily Dickinson: Variorum Edition* (Belknap Press, 1998), Fr1513A, as published in the [Emily Dickinson Archive](https://curiosity.lib.harvard.edu/emily-dickinson-archive/catalog/195-EDA2078_F1513A).

**She left herself alternatives, and the first editors took them.** Franklin records three words Dickinson wrote in as options: *denote* for “imply” in line 5, *designate* for “intimate” in line 6, and *What customs* for “What function” in line 8. When the poem was first printed in *Poems* (1896) it appeared **as three quatrains, with the alternatives for lines 5 and 8 adopted** — so the version that circulated read *denote* and *What customs*, and the version above is the one on the paper.

Neither reading is a mistake. She wrote both. But an editor choosing between a poet’s alternatives, silently, and printing the result as the poem is the same move as removing her dashes, and it is the move this collection keeps finding. **The alternatives are the poem too.** A text that has had its options resolved for you is a text with a decision hidden in it.

‘Tis Drama — if Hypothesis It be not Tragedy

## She kept a herbarium, which is what this site is

Dickinson assembled more than four hundred pressed plants as a young woman, mounted and labelled, and the album is now in Harvard’s Houghton Library — the same library that holds the manuscript on [Sheet No. 6](https://queering.earth/wild-nights). *Monotropa uniflora* is in it.

This site is drawn as a herbarium sheet because the form makes an attribution argument: a specimen is somebody else’s, a label is where we speak, and the line between them is drawn in the layout rather than left to a reader’s good faith. **It is a slightly strange thing to discover that the poet on two of our sheets was doing the same thing at nineteen**, with real plants, in an album, in Amherst.

Which is also the answer to the question people keep asking about her life. From outside it looked like a withdrawal. From the letters, the poems, and four hundred labelled specimens, it looks like the opposite: attention pooled, at length, on a small number of things, with enormous care. There is a word for that now, and the word shares a root with the flower.

## Not a tragedy

The plant is white because it has given up chlorophyll. It has no leaves. It grows in the dark, on the forest floor, out of leaf litter, and it feeds through fungi that feed through trees. By every measure a plant is usually judged by, it is failing at being a plant.

It is also perfectly well. It is not a parasite on trees and not a saprophyte on rot, which is what botanists thought for a century; it is a myco-heterotroph, and the arrangement works. **The plant is not doing without a connection to light. It is connected to light through somebody else.** That is not a lesser way to be alive, and Star Stuff has the numbers on how the carbon actually moves.

Dickinson’s last line does not say the thing is a tragedy. It says: “‘Tis Drama - if Hypothesis / It be not Tragedy -” — which reads, turned around, as a hope with a condition on it. Helen puts the same thought without the subjunctive: the ghost pipe is not a tragedy, and neither are Autistic people, and both thrive when the conditions are right rather than when they are corrected.

What this sheet will not tidy

- **We are not claiming Dickinson was Autistic**, and neither is Helen — she says so in as many words on her own page. Monotropism is a theory of attention that many Autistic people recognise; a nineteenth-century poet cannot be assessed by resemblance, and reading her life through a word coined in 1991 is our doing, not hers.
- **The rhyme between the plant and the theory is a coincidence of vocabulary, not evidence of anything.** Linnaeus named a stem’s curve. Murray and Buirski named a pattern of attention. That both reached for monotropos is lovely and it proves nothing about either.
- This sheet has **no plate**. Every mounted image on this site is a public-domain botanical print or painting, and we do not have one of *Monotropa uniflora*. The Dickinson manuscript is available but licensed, the modern photographs are in copyright, and Todd’s painted panel — the object at the centre of the letter — we could not clear. **If you know of a public-domain *Monotropa uniflora* plate**, it belongs here. [Say so](https://github.com/Stimpunks/Queering-Earth/issues) and it will be.
- The plant blackens and collapses when handled, and Helen reads that as recognisable. We have kept her reading in her words rather than generalising it, because “maybe it’s just me who relates in this way” is in her sentence and taking it out would make a shared claim out of a personal one.
- **The biology here is deliberately thin.** Myco-heterotrophy is a mechanism with numbers attached and those belong to our sibling site, which risks a wrong fact where this one risks a wrong attribution. If you want to know how the carbon moves, [go there](https://starstuff.earth/symbioses-field-guide.html).

Dinah Murray spent her last years photographing lichens and mushrooms on the Fife coast — the same kingdom of organisms this plant lives through, attended to closely, for their own sake, by someone who had given the world a word for exactly that kind of attention. Kate Fox called the memorial poem *Monotropa Uniflora*. It was the right name.

Queering Earth Sheet No. 8 Accessioned 9 Sep 2026

Provenance Mounted [9 September 2026](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-09-patina). [Label corrected once before it shipped](https://queering.earth/changelog#a-2026-09-09-patina) — a quotation on the essay this sheet follows is credited to the wrong book, and it is credited here to the right one.

# What this cabinet is for

https://queering.earth/mission
The founding papers · updated 2026-09-09

[Queering Earth](https://queering.earth/) · The founding papers

# What this cabinet is for

Thirteen aims, and where each one is already kept.

This site has a page for what it holds, a page for how it is made, a page for everything it has got wrong, and a page for what it knows about you. What it did not have was a page saying, plainly and in one place, what we are *trying to do*. That absence is not neutral: a project with no stated aim is a project whose aims can drift without anybody being able to point at the drift — which is the same objection this site makes to a quotation nobody can trace, or a number nobody can re-derive.

## The whole of it, in one sentence

Queering Earth reads the canon closely and in public — art, literature, poetry, politics, people, and history — and asks what else any of it could have been, so that the arrangements we were handed stop looking like the only ones available.

Thirteen aims follow, in four groups. **None of them is a hope.** Each one names a page where it is already being practised, because a values list you cannot check against the work is the exact thing this page is trying not to be. And [the last section](#stopped) names, for each, the observation that would show we had quietly stopped.

## What we are claiming

1.  **Queering is a verb.** The word reaches us from Queer Theory by way of [Nick Walker](https://neuroqueer.com/), and what we took is the parenthesis: *subverting, defying, disrupting, liberating oneself from*. It names something you *do* to a norm, not a category you belong to, and the norms it can be done to are not only the ones about sex and gender. A site that used the word as a synonym for a demographic would be using the noun and calling it the verb. Kept on [Queering is a verb](https://queering.earth/#queering-is-a-verb), where he is quoted exactly rather than paraphrased.
2.  **Normal is an invention, and a recent one.** Barely two centuries old, arriving with the statistician rather than the physician, and it displaced older words that meant something else entirely — *wyrd* meant *fate*, what befalls you, before it was demoted to *weird* and then to defect. **A thing that was invented can be read as an invention**, which is a different act from complaining about it. Kept on [Sheet No. 4](https://queering.earth/invention-of-normal), and it is Helen Edgar’s reading before it is this site’s.
3.  **Having been canonised is not the same as having been settled.** Every sheet takes a work that has already been decided about and asks what else it could have been. Not to catch anybody out — the readings here are affectionate, and several are love letters. But a text that can only be read one way has stopped being a text and become a ruling. Kept on [the plate](https://queering.earth/#what-grows-here), one sheet at a time.

## How we intend to be right

4.  **Interpretation is the method, and the room left open is the product.** There are no hard facts here for everything, and that is the design brief rather than a lowered bar. Our sibling [Star Stuff](https://starstuff.earth/) is built on evidence and risks a wrong fact; this half of the shelf is built on reading and risks a wrong attribution. What replaces the fact is not licence. It is the obligation to **show the reading’s working**, so that somebody can disagree with it precisely rather than vaguely. Kept on [What this is](https://queering.earth/#what-this-is), and argued in full on [the colophon](https://queering.earth/design#model).
5.  **If we changed the words, they are ours.** The characteristic failure on a site like this is not an invented source. It is a *tightened* one — a definition trimmed to fit a masthead, an object quietly generalised, a paraphrase left wearing somebody’s name. So: credit the concept, quote the original exactly, or write our own line. When we carry somebody’s idea to an object they were not writing about, **the sheet says whose move that is** instead of letting their authority cover our argument. Kept in [the attribution ledger](https://queering.earth/ledger) — see the Tuck and Yang entry, where the transposition is named on the sheet in a sentence of its own.
6.  **Every quotation reaches the page from a primary, or names whose transcription it is.** A search of our own library is not verification: five files agreeing with each other are one witness, not five. Where the primary can be reached we read it and say which copy, because that is how an edition difference gets caught. Where it cannot, the quotation carries the citation and the name of whoever transcribed it, rather than being dropped or quietly smoothed. Kept in [the ledger](https://queering.earth/ledger), each entry dated the day a person read the source.
7.  **Publish the corrections, and spend the gold on the mend.** Every sheet carries at its foot the date it was mounted and the number of times we have corrected it since, each clause linked to the entry that did it. The seam is marked in the most expensive colour the palette has, because *kintsugi* is not that the crack shows — it is that the precious material goes on the break. **A register with no corrections in it is not a clean record. It is a record nobody is keeping.** Kept in [the accession register](https://queering.earth/changelog), and on the provenance line at the foot of every sheet.
8.  **A reading is signed, and the reader is not the maker.** Woolf made *On Being Ill*; we made the reading of it. Those are two different people, on two different rows of the label and in two different fields of the machine-readable copy, and no page here collapses them into one name at the top. Getting that wrong would tell every agent on the web that we wrote Woolf. Kept on [Who reads, and who writes](https://queering.earth/design#who-writes), and enforced by a gate that refuses the conflation.

## What we owe whoever is reading

9.  **One document, and two ways to read it.** The type here leans, deviates, and refuses to sit on the line, because a page about normativity set in a tidy grid is arguing against itself. All of that lives in the stylesheet, over ordinary semantic markup, and **plain view switches it off**. Never an image of text. Never a decorative copy beside an accessible one — two copies of the same words drift, and the accessible one is always the copy that rots. Kept on [Plain view](https://queering.earth/design#plain-view), and on the control at the top of this page.
10.  **Accessibility measured, not asserted.** Contrast is held at 7:1 in both grounds and under print emulation — the house target, not the 4.5:1 floor. Every page has one landmark, real headings, an address for every section, and a printable sheet. None of that is a promise: each claim is checked by a gate that runs before anything ships, and the gates are in the repository where you can run them yourself. Kept on [How it is built](https://queering.earth/design#built), and in [the tools directory](https://github.com/Stimpunks/Queering-Earth/tree/main/tools).
11.  **Ask nothing of you.** No analytics, no cookies, no accounts, no comments, no advertising, no newsletter gate, and nothing fetched from anybody else’s server unless you press something that says so first. The one field on the site never submits anywhere, and what you search for stays in your own browser. Kept on [What this site knows about you](https://queering.earth/privacy), which is checked against the code every time the code grows a capability.

## How we work

12.  **In public, with the working-out left in.** The pages, the drawings, the tools, the gates, the attribution ledger, the decision log and every error we have caught in our own work are one public repository at one commit. The register records not only what we mounted but what we took down again and why. Nothing here is finished in private and then presented. Kept in [the repository](https://github.com/Stimpunks/Queering-Earth) and in [the register](https://queering.earth/changelog).
13.  **Free, forkable, and yes to the machines.** Everything of ours is [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/); the works we read belong to the people who made them and were never ours to license. The training crawlers and the retrieval crawlers are named in `robots.txt` and **allowed**, because a refusal beside a share-alike licence would be a contradiction somebody would eventually have to resolve. **The answer is yes and the ask is attribution** — so the citation trail is published in the form a machine can actually reach. Kept in [robots.txt](https://queering.earth/robots.txt), in [llms.txt](https://queering.earth/llms.txt), and in a Markdown copy beside every page.

## What a cabinet of readings has to do with Stimpunks

Queering Earth is a collaboration between the [Stimpunks Foundation](https://stimpunks.org/) and [More Realms](https://morerealms.com/). Stimpunks is a 501(c)(3) with a mission of its own, published on its own site, and it is worth quoting rather than paraphrasing — the paraphrase is where a mission usually goes soft, and paraphrase-wearing-a-name is the failure this whole site is organised against.

Specimen — the foundation’s own words

> We exist for the direct support and mutual aid of neurodivergent and disabled people.

> Stimpunks builds accessible infrastructure and public tools that support disabled and neurodivergent people to live with dignity, challenge dehumanizing systems, and design environments that honor difference as strength.

> We enable the weird, feral, chaotic, and magical people.

Stimpunks Foundation, [*Mission*](https://stimpunks.org/mission/), read 9 September 2026. Their capitalisation and their spelling.

**The middle sentence has three verbs in it, and this site is a contribution to each one.** *Live with dignity* is what a reading does when it hands somebody a word for themselves that is not a deficit. *Challenge dehumanizing systems* is what Sheet No. 4 does to “normal” and Sheet No. 1 does to the army you desert by lying down. *Design environments that honor difference as strength* is the reason the type on this site plays and the reason plain view exists in the same breath.

The third sentence is the one that surprised us. **Stimpunks’ own mission says “weird”** — and [Sheet No. 4](https://queering.earth/invention-of-normal) is the history of exactly that word being demoted from *wyrd*, meaning fate, to a name for people who do not fit. The sheet was not written to illustrate the mission. It turned out to be about it.

## And what it has to do with More Realms

The other half is [Helen Edgar](https://morerealms.com/)’s, and her own landing page states the method this site borrowed before this site existed.

Specimen — the other masthead

> This is not a place of conclusions or answers, it’s a place to wander, to feel, to think sideways, expand, explore and be inspired.

Helen Edgar, [More Realms](https://morerealms.com/), landing page, read 9 September 2026. Her punctuation.

“Not a place of conclusions or answers” is the same commitment this site makes when it says there are no hard facts here for everything, arrived at from her side rather than ours. **The tagline on the masthead is hers** — “post-normal possibilities”, written in the founding brainstorm — and the masthead credits Nick Walker beneath it because his book carries the phrase as a subtitle, one hyphen apart. That credit is not an admission of borrowing and does not claim one; it is what you do when a collision is real and a reader will eventually find it.

## The limit, said plainly

What this site does not do Stimpunks’ first programme is direct financial support to individuals — rent, medical bills, equipment, creator grants, living wages. **This site does none of that and should not be counted as though it did.** No sheet here has paid anybody’s rent or replaced anybody’s wheelchair. If anything on these pages is worth something to you, the thing that converts it into material help is [the foundation](https://stimpunks.org/), not the artifact.

The honest claim for a cabinet of readings is narrower, and still worth making. It is what somebody can reach at two in the morning, free, without an account, in a browser, when they have just been told again that the way they are is a defect — and find a page that takes the question seriously enough to cite its sources.

## How you could tell if we stopped

**An aim you cannot fail is not an aim.** Each of these is a condition somebody could observe from outside, with no access to what we meant, which is the only sort of accountability worth publishing.

The aim, and the observation that would falsify it

| Aim | What would show we had stopped |
| --- | --- |
| Queering is a verb | The word used here as a synonym for a demographic, or as something a person *is* rather than something done to a norm. |
| --- | --- |
| Canonised is not settled | A sheet that arrives at the verdict the work already had, and adds nothing to it but agreement. |
| --- | --- |
| The room left open | A sheet that closes its reading — that tells you what the poem *means* rather than what it could mean, and leaves you nothing to disagree with. |
| --- | --- |
| If we changed the words | A quotation here that does not match its source, with the source’s name still attached. Or our extension of somebody’s idea presented as their reach rather than ours. |
| --- | --- |
| Primary sources | A citation trail that ends at a quote site, an encyclopedia, one of our own pages, or a machine’s summary. |
| --- | --- |
| Publish the corrections | A stretch of the register with no corrections in it. We are not that good; a clean run means we stopped looking. |
| --- | --- |
| Reader is not the maker | A page whose byline or metadata names us as the author of the work being read. |
| --- | --- |
| One document | Anything readable only in the decorated version, or an image with words in it that the words are not also in. |
| --- | --- |
| Measured, not asserted | A contrast failure shipped and left standing, a page that comes off a printer blank, or a gate quietly run without its checking flag. |
| --- | --- |
| Ask nothing of you | Any request to a third party that the reader did not choose, or any attempt to find out who is reading. |
| --- | --- |
| In public | A count printed in our prose that nobody can re-derive from the repository. |
| --- | --- |

**Most of those are not hypothetical, and the ones that have already happened here are the reason the list reads the way it does.** This site’s working tagline was once a paraphrase of Nick Walker wearing his name, and it was replaced. Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang were carried from settler colonialism to masking, and the sheet nearly let their authority cover the move before it was made to say so in a sentence of its own. The plate said “Seven sheets” above eight cards for as long as the eighth had been up — a count in our prose that nobody could re-derive, which is the last row of that table, committed by us, on this site, and found only because somebody read down the page and counted.

Every one of those is in [the register](https://queering.earth/changelog) with a date on it. That is the point of keeping one.

## Who wrote this, and with what

The reading, the editing, and the deciding are Helen Edgar’s and Ryan Boren’s; the drafting is done in sessions with an AI assistant, directed and edited by whichever of them is answerable for the sheet. **A tool does not get a row on the label, because a byline is responsibility and a tool cannot carry any** — but a site that keeps a ledger of everybody else’s words owes an honest account of where its own came from, so the arrangement is described rather than left to be inferred.

The full statement, including what is never allowed to stand as a citation, is on [the colophon](https://queering.earth/design#who-writes).
